title: Advancing Spatial Health Inequalities Research: Innovations in Data, Methods, and Theory—Special Issue Introduction
authors: Höhn, A., Heppenstall, A., & Lomax, N.

summary.background: Inequalities in population health between and within areas remain a feature of societies across the world, and many are rooted in long-standing disparities in the distribution of and access to the resources that shape health. Decades of research and policy effort have not shifted them; some have widened. This editorial introduces a special issue that gathers innovations in data, methods and theory intended to deepen understanding of these persistent spatial inequalities, and sets out the common threads running through the contributions.
summary.importance: Spatial health inequalities research is increasingly interdisciplinary, drawing on spatial econometrics, health geography, demography and systems science. We frame the special issue around what these traditions share once combined: a recognition that place is partly a social and political construct, that coarse geographies obscure meaningful variation, and that causal claims are hard to sustain in spatial settings. Positioning the collection this way gives readers an honest account of where the field's methods can and cannot go.
summary.methods: As an editorial, we review eight contributions and draw out shared concerns rather than presenting new analysis. The papers span causal inference in spatial econometrics, machine-learning approaches to deprivation and pandemic preparedness, space–time clustering, unobserved heterogeneity, GIS-based accessibility modelling, welfare-state comparison and life-expectancy decomposition.
summary.findings: Causality is the recurring limitation: spatial interdependence violates assumptions central to causal identification, so consistency in causal language matters, and co-occurrence and mechanism can still be interpreted carefully without it. We also flag the collection's focus on high-income countries as a gap. Narrowing real-world inequalities, we argue, will depend on translating evidence into policy and political will.

title: Calibrating a Global Trade Agent-Based Model with an HPC–ABC–SMC Framework
authors: Li, K., Ge, J., Lomax, N., & Polhill, J. G.
journal: Journal of Artificial Societies and Social Simulation

summary.background: Agent-based models are well suited to systems of heterogeneous actors that produce system-level patterns, such as global trade, but fitting them to empirical data is computationally expensive. Bayesian calibration through Approximate Bayesian Computation with Sequential Monte Carlo (ABC-SMC) returns parameter uncertainty rather than a single best fit, yet most workflows couple the statistical sampler to the model through interface tools such as PyNetLogo or RNetLogo. That coupling adds serialisation overhead at every inference step and limits parallelisation on high-performance computing (HPC) clusters, so calibrating a computationally intensive model to real data stays out of reach for many applied modellers. This paper builds and tests a framework that separates simulation from inference, applied to a global food trade model.
summary.importance: A calibration method that returns full posterior distributions, rather than a single best-fit parameter set, lets modellers quantify how much confidence to place in each parameter, which matters when a model is used to inform policy analysis. The core idea, decoupling simulation from inference through a precomputed lookup table, is an architectural pattern that carries over to any simulation platform supporting batch execution, so the contribution is not specific to trade. For trade research, the calibrated model puts quantitative weight on how far current flows are shaped by historical links against endogenous partner search.
summary.methods: The proposed framework, HPC-ABC-SMC, splits each ABC-SMC generation into two stages. First, all required NetLogo simulations run as independent HPC tasks, with their outputs aggregated into a parameter–output lookup table. Second, ABC-SMC inference runs locally by querying that table, with no further calls to NetLogo. The decoupling removes repeated interface overhead and allows task-level parallelisation across simulation batches. We applied the framework to a global food trade model with three calibration parameters (weights on initial trade, endogenous trade and GDP per capita) across 8 to 10 generations, using FAO trade data covering all 97 commodity categories. Two objectives were calibrated separately: matching trade partners and matching trade volumes. Results were cross-validated against a genetic algorithm, and a sensitivity analysis assessed the influence of each parameter.
summary.findings: Decoupling simulation from inference gave up to a 42-fold reduction in wall-clock time relative to GUI-based single-core execution while preserving the statistical rigour of the calibration, and returned full posteriors with 95% credible intervals. The genetic algorithm's single best-fit solution for each objective fell inside the corresponding ABC-SMC credible interval, confirming the posterior estimates. The two objectives behaved differently: partner-matching converged to small parameter magnitudes with tight intervals, indicating that partner choice is governed mainly by endogenous search, whereas volume-matching required a much larger weight on historical trade links (posterior mean 18.29), giving quantitative support to path dependence in trade networks. GDP per capita weight was the most influential parameter, with strong nonlinear interactions across the three weights. Posterior means deviate by 20 to 45% from the earlier point calibration of Ge et al. (2021), and some literature values sit inside one objective's credible interval but outside the other's, which shows the value of uncertainty-aware calibration over single-point fitting. The paper is led by PhD student Kejian Li, whom Nik Lomax supervises as primary supervisor.

title: A multilevel analysis of pupils' travel distance to primary school: Simultaneously modelling origins and destinations
authors: Huang, H., Gould, M., Lomax, N., & Yang, J.

summary.background: The distance children travel to school is both an indicator of educational equity and a determinant of wellbeing, but most analyses model only the home neighbourhood or only the school, missing the joint structure of origins and destinations. In China, where the hukou (household registration) system ties school eligibility to officially registered residence with different rules for local and non-local registrants, the contribution of hukou status to travel distance, and how it interacts with school type and neighbourhood characteristics, had not been examined in a framework that respects both geographies. This paper modelled the travel distances of primary school pupils in a Chinese urban setting using cross-classified multilevel models that account simultaneously for the home neighbourhood and the school attended.
summary.importance: Cross-classified multilevel models accommodate the fact that pupils are embedded in two distinct hierarchies at once, so they correct the bias that nested-only models carry and expose cross-level interactions that nested designs cannot detect. Applied to the hukou question, the framework gives Chinese policymakers a sharper read on how registration-based enrolment shapes school accessibility, and how the gap between local and non-local hukou holders varies by neighbourhood density. The same approach transfers to any setting where pupils' lives sit in non-nested origin and destination geographies.
summary.methods: We used data on a sample of primary school pupils in a Chinese urban setting, with information on each pupil's home neighbourhood, school attended, hukou status, family characteristics and the distance from home to school. Pupils were modelled with cross-classified multilevel models that allow each pupil to belong simultaneously to one home neighbourhood and one school, with random effects at both levels capturing the unexplained variance contributed by each. We also estimated nested models that respect either origin or destination structure, and we tested cross-level interactions between pupil-level variables (notably hukou status) and contextual variables at neighbourhood and school level, including school type and neighbourhood population density.
summary.findings: Pupils' travel distances are shaped by individual factors and by contextual factors at both home neighbourhood and school. Hukou status emerged as an important individual-level factor, with non-local hukou holders typically travelling differently from local hukou holders, and the relationship was mediated by school type. A cross-level interaction between neighbourhood population density and hukou status was also detected, with the gap between local and non-local hukou holders varying by density. The findings underline the role of hukou-based enrolment in shaping school accessibility and suggest that reform of enrolment policy is a priority for advancing educational equity. The cross-classified multilevel approach is suitable for similar questions wherever pupils are embedded in distinct origin and destination geographies.

title: Measuring the accessibility of veterinary care for companion animals in England and Wales
authors: Clark, S., Clarke, G., James, W., & Lomax, N.

summary.background: A Competition and Markets Authority investigation into the UK veterinary services market has highlighted concerns about ownership concentration, rising fees and limited local choice for the half of UK households who own a pet. Existing estimates of UK pet ownership sit at coarse postal geographies and cover restricted species at earlier time points, and the accessibility literature has not systematically applied supply-weighted travel-time measures to companion animal care, so the question of where additional veterinary capacity is most needed cannot currently be answered. This paper estimated the pet population at neighbourhood scale across England and Wales, combined this with data on veterinary practice locations and travel times, and mapped accessibility to identify potential "veterinary deserts".
summary.importance: A small-area accessibility map of veterinary care gives animal welfare bodies, regulators and the CMA a concrete basis for identifying where additional capacity should be prioritised, with potential knock-on effects on the cost of care through increased local competition. The combination of spatial microsimulation for demand and supply-weighted travel time for access is methodologically transferable to other countries with comparable data, and to other services where small-area access matters for outcomes.
summary.methods: We used spatial microsimulation, which combines survey microdata on pet-owning households with area-level constraints from census and administrative sources, to estimate the household pet population at neighbourhood level across the 36,672 neighbourhoods of England and Wales, each containing roughly 700 households. We then assembled data on the location of veterinary practices and the number of veterinarians at each. Accessibility was measured by combining pet demand with veterinary supply weighted by vehicle journey times between neighbourhoods and practices, producing a measure for each neighbourhood. We mapped the results at national scale and zoomed in on a case-study town (Barnsley, South Yorkshire) to illustrate finer-grained variation.
summary.findings: Accessibility to veterinary care varied substantially across England and Wales. More affluent and rural locations tended to have better accessibility than deprived and urban ones, identifying the latter as candidate "veterinary deserts" where additional capacity could be prioritised. The case study showed how the picture varies at within-town scale, with the level of access depending on both proximity to practices and local pet density. The findings give animal welfare bodies, regulators and policymakers a basis for targeting interventions to improve access, with potential knock-on effects on the affordability of care through increased local competition. The method can be applied wherever comparable data on pet ownership and veterinary supply exist.

title: Do Welfare Regimes Matter? A Comparative Analysis of Area-Level Inequalities in Life Expectancy in Germany and the United Kingdom, 2003–2021
authors: Mühlichen, M., Höhn, A., Lomax, N., Meier, P., & Grigoriev, P.

summary.background: Area-level inequalities in life expectancy are well documented within individual countries but cross-national comparisons are rare. Within-country studies are common, but the implicit age standardisation of life expectancy makes cross-country area-level comparison feasible, and that opportunity had not been taken for two textbook welfare regimes (the liberal UK and the conservative Germany) across two recent decades that include austerity and the COVID-19 pandemic. This paper estimated and compared district-level life expectancy inequalities in the UK and Germany over 2003 to 2021.
summary.importance: A direct UK–Germany comparison turns welfare-regime theory into testable area-level evidence: with similar headline life expectancy and demographics, any divergence in sub-national inequality is hard to attribute to anything other than the way each state organises the provision of equitable living conditions. The slope index of inequality applied to district-level deprivation deciles gives a single, comparable measure of the gap in each country across two decades, and the framework transfers to other country pairs that map cleanly onto contrasting welfare regimes.
summary.methods: We used mortality data from national statistical offices to estimate life expectancy for all districts in the UK and Germany for the period 2003 to 2021. Districts in both countries are comparable units of local government with similar functions, allowing direct comparison. We assigned each district a deprivation decile based on employment data, with deciles defined within each country, and calculated life expectancy for each decile. The magnitude of inequality across deciles was summarised using the slope index of inequality, a standard measure that captures the gradient of an outcome across an ordered socio-economic distribution. We compared temporal trends in the slope index in both countries, paying particular attention to periods of austerity and the first years of the COVID-19 pandemic.
summary.findings: Average district-level life expectancy was similar in the two countries, but the UK consistently showed higher area-level inequality than Germany across the studied period. District-level inequalities in life expectancy increased in both countries over time, but the rise was steeper in the UK and accelerated further during the first years of the COVID-19 pandemic. The findings are consistent with deeply rooted differences in how the two welfare regimes approach the provision of equitable living conditions across their sub-national territories, and support the view that welfare state arrangements are a useful frame for understanding why countries with similar headline life expectancy can differ markedly in the area-level inequalities behind that headline.

title: The "AIP" Framework: Sharing learnings from a case study of a successful Academic Industry data sharing Partnership
authors: Jenneson, V., Stone, R. A., Ennis, E., Naisbitt, R., Lomax, N., & Morris, M. A.

summary.background: Commercial smart data offer social research opportunities that survey data cannot, but academia-industry data sharing partnerships for social research remain rare and hard to establish. Existing frameworks for inter-organisational collaboration assume data ownership and decision authority sit in the same place, which is not the case when commercial data are shared with academia, and little practical guidance exists on initiating, sustaining and benefiting from such partnerships. This paper used a case study of an established partnership between the University of Leeds and a large UK supermarket to identify what made it work, and to develop a preliminary framework that other teams can use.
summary.importance: The AIP framework gives academic and industry partners a structured way to think about the conditions a data sharing partnership needs before any data move (shared goals, co-production culture, trust-based governance), the governance under which sharing operates, the research process that turns the data into insight, and the strategic work that sustains the relationship. Set against the DIKW Pyramid extended for two organisations, it makes visible the people-and-process elements that determine whether commercial smart data actually deliver social-research value, and is reusable by other universities and businesses contemplating similar partnerships.
summary.methods: The study was qualitative and exploratory. We conducted ten semi-structured online interviews with participants drawn from both sides of the partnership: six from the University of Leeds research team and four from the supermarket, covering roles across the data sharing process from legal and governance through to senior leadership. Interviews followed a schedule structured around the DIKW Pyramid extended with sub-themes for cross-organisation working. Transcripts were analysed using deductive reflexive thematic analysis, with a-priori themes drawn from the DIKW Pyramid and additional inductive themes allowed to emerge. The research team included members of the partnership and an external researcher, and findings were shared with the supermarket for validation.
summary.findings: The analysis produced the Academia-Industry Partnership (AIP) framework, which extends the DIKW Pyramid for two-organisation data sharing partnerships. It comprises four components: a Research Infrastructure Foundation of shared goals, co-production culture and trust-based governance, established before any project begins; a Data Sharing Process that operationalises that foundation under formal governance; a Research Process that captures the journey from raw data to actionable insight within each project; and an overarching Partnership Strategy that nurtures relationships across all components. Key practical insights include the centrality of people and personal relationships, the value of regular two-way communication, the risks posed by staff turnover, and the importance of strategic oversight to avoid siloed working as partnerships scale. The framework is offered as a preliminary tool to support other academic and industry teams in designing similar collaborations.

title: Is Germany experiencing urban or suburban growth? Contrasting long-standing and novel urban gradient classifications
authors: Kolowa, T. J., Weigand, M., Standfuß, I., Klüsener, S., Lomax, N., & Taubenböck, H.

summary.background: Whether a country is experiencing urban or suburban growth depends both on the underlying demographics and on how urban, suburban and rural areas are classified. Empirical accounts have used administrative boundaries or commuting data, neither of which captures urban morphology directly, and although remote sensing and gridded population data have produced novel morphology-based classifications, no systematic comparison against established schemes had been carried out for Germany or other European countries. This paper compared three contrasting classifications of the urban-rural gradient and used them to assess population change in 50 German metropolitan regions between 2011 and 2022.
summary.importance: Direct comparison of morphology-based, population-based and functional classifications shows which conclusions about urban and suburban growth are classification-robust and which depend on the scheme chosen. That gives policymakers and demographers a clear reading of how much weight to put on different sources of evidence in the renewed-suburbanisation debate, and it gives researchers a transferable framework: the same comparison runs in any country where comparable demographic and remote-sensing data exist.
summary.methods: We compared three urban gradient classifications applied to 50 metropolitan regions in Germany over the period 2011 to 2022. The morphology-based classification uses three-dimensional building volume data derived from remote sensing to delineate urban, suburban and peri-urban areas by built form. The population-based classification draws on high-resolution gridded population data and density thresholds. The functional classification follows established administrative practice, using commuting-tied delineations of urban regions. For each classification we computed population growth rates in each band of the gradient at the national scale and at the level of the individual metropolitan region, and compared the resulting trend patterns across classifications.
summary.findings: At the national scale, all three classifications point to a similar story: urban areas grew faster than suburban or peri-urban areas across the period. At the regional scale, however, the picture varied: classifications agreed in some metropolitan regions and disagreed in others, with the trend assigned to a given region sometimes depending on the classification chosen. Methodological choices about how the urban gradient is delineated therefore matter for regional findings but not so much for the national-level conclusion in this case. The framework can be applied to other countries with comparable data, and the results show that policy debates about suburbanisation at sub-national scale need to specify the classification on which they rest.

title: Examining the cost of living crisis: insights from e-petitions and constituency groupings
authors: Clark, S. D., & Lomax, N.
journal: Handbook on Governance and Data Science

summary.background: The recent cost of living crisis pushed UK inflation in essentials well above target and squeezed real incomes. Earlier e-petition work had classified UK constituencies on broader issues and on COVID-19, but the cost-of-living crisis had not been examined this way, and conventional constituency-level polling is too slow and expensive to support the policy feedback loop during a slow-moving economic crisis. This chapter used signatures to UK Parliament e-petitions submitted during the crisis to identify the topics that animated public concern, to classify constituencies by the cost-of-living concerns most pronounced among their residents, and to explore the political and social character of the resulting groupings.
summary.importance: UK Parliament e-petitions are addressed to government, carry verified named signatures and are tied to specific residential constituencies, so they deliver a near-real-time, constituency-scale signal of which crisis concerns voters are pressing government on. A topic-modelled classification turns that signal into a usable map of where particular concerns (energy, food, tax, benefits, housing) concentrate, and how those concentrations relate to party-political and social divides. The approach can be re-run as new petitions arrive and adapted to other crises and other legislatures with comparable petitioning systems.
summary.methods: We assembled signatures to UK Parliament e-petitions submitted during the cost of living crisis period that addressed cost-of-living themes, retaining those debated in Parliament. Petition text was modelled using a topic-modelling approach that represents documents as mixtures of latent topics derived from word co-occurrence, with the number of topics chosen by standard model-fit metrics. Each petition was assigned to its most probable topic, and topics were grouped into broader thematic collections covering energy, food, taxation, benefits, housing and related concerns. For each topic we computed a measure of constituency support based on the share of signatures, and applied a classification method to group constituencies with similar topic profiles. We then characterised the groupings geographically, politically and against general election outcomes.
summary.findings: The topic models identified a set of distinct concerns within the cost-of-living petition corpus, covering domestic energy prices, food costs, taxation, benefit policy and housing affordability among others. A small number of constituency groupings emerged, differing in which topics their residents engaged with most strongly. The groupings overlapped with political voting patterns and with social characteristics but were not reducible to either. The findings show that e-petition data can be used to map public concerns during a slow-moving economic crisis at fine geographic scale, providing a rolling indicator that complements polling and economic statistics for both policymakers and political parties.

title: An Inclusive Economy Classification of British Local Authority Districts and Assessment of Its Association With Life Expectancy and Lifespan Variation
authors: Lomax, N., Rice, H. P., Höhn, A., Hughes, C., Heppenstall, A., Elsenbroich, C., & Meier, P.

summary.background: Economic inclusion is increasingly recognised as a driver of health inequalities. But no systematic classification of British Local Authority Districts by inclusivity exists, so whether more inclusive places really are healthier has not been tested at the scale relevant to local policy. This paper built such a classification at Local Authority District level and assessed how the resulting groups differ in life expectancy and lifespan variation.
summary.importance: The inclusive economy concept covers employment and pay alongside access to services, connectivity, housing affordability and civic participation: substantially more than the deprivation indices the field has relied on. Pairing the classification with both life expectancy and lifespan variation (a measure of inequality in age at death) gives a fuller picture of population health than either measure alone. The dataset gives policymakers and researchers a tool for targeting investment, modelling intervention scenarios and assessing where the joint relationship between inclusion and health is weakest.
summary.methods: We drew on 13 indicators of the inclusive economy across two domains: economic outcomes (employment, pay, poverty, job security, earnings inequality) and wider enablers (skills, digital and physical connectivity, housing affordability, civic participation), harmonised across England, Scotland and Wales for 2017 to 2021. After multiple imputation and standardisation, we applied k-means clustering, which groups areas with similar profiles across all indicators simultaneously. The number of clusters was chosen on conceptual, spatial and health-outcome grounds, supported by statistical diagnostics. Life expectancy and lifespan variation at birth came from life tables built on modelled age-specific mortality rates.
summary.findings: Four clusters emerged: less economically inclusive, more economically inclusive, average, and a polarised mix of extremes concentrated largely in London. Across three of the four clusters the pattern was consistent: the least inclusive areas had the lowest life expectancy and the highest lifespan variation, the most inclusive the opposite. The London-dominated cluster was the exception, recording relatively high life expectancy alongside high lifespan variation, suggesting a polarisation of lifespans driven by the area's socio-economic diversity. The clusters captured more than deprivation alone. The findings point to a double disadvantage in less economically inclusive areas, suggesting place-based policies targeting economic inclusion as a route to reducing health inequalities.

title: An inclusive economy dataset for wards in Great Britain using administrative and synthetic data sources
authors: Rice, H. P., Höhn, A., Meier, P., Heppenstall, A., & Lomax, N.

summary.background: Policymakers planning local interventions on economic inclusion need data at fine spatial scale. But UK datasets on the local economy focus on deprivation indices that differ between England, Scotland and Wales, and the only available inclusive economy dataset is published at Local Authority District scale, which is too coarse for many policy uses. This paper constructed a harmonised dataset of 13 inclusive economy indicators at electoral ward level for Great Britain for 2019 to 2021, and documented its construction, validation and intended uses.
summary.importance: Ward-level coverage opens up local-area analysis of economic inclusion at a scale much closer to the lived experience of communities, and the inclusion of age-standardised SF-12 mental and physical health summary scores in the same dataset lets users link inclusivity to population health directly. The use of the SIPHER Synthetic Population to fill indicators not available at fine scale shows what is possible when synthetic methods supplement administrative open data, and the published validation against deprivation indices and external reference sources lets users judge how far the dataset can be trusted for their purpose.
summary.methods: We assembled 13 indicators of the inclusive economy across two domains: economic outcomes such as employment, earnings inequality, poverty and job security; and wider enablers such as skills, connectivity, housing affordability and civic participation. Where administrative open data covered the indicator at fine scale, we used it directly. For variables only available at coarser scale or for individuals, we used the SIPHER Synthetic Population, a validated synthetic micro dataset for Great Britain, to estimate ward-level values consistent with both census totals and Understanding Society survey distributions. Indicators were harmonised across England, Scotland and Wales on 2022 electoral ward boundaries. The dataset also includes age-standardised SF-12 mental and physical health summary scores at the ward level and supplementary demographic indicators. We validated the dataset against deprivation indices and other reference data sources.
summary.findings: The dataset covers nearly all wards in Great Britain across the 13 inclusive economy indicators for 2019 to 2021, alongside ward-level mental and physical health summary measures. Comparisons against deprivation indices and external reference data show that the dataset is consistent where overlap exists and adds information where it does not, supporting its use for research and policy at granular spatial scale. The dataset complements the earlier Local Authority District version produced by the SIPHER consortium and gives policymakers, researchers and practitioners a resource for studying economic inclusion at a scale appropriate to local intervention design and evaluation.

title: Estimating quality-adjusted life expectancy (QALE) for local authorities in Great Britain and its association with indicators of the inclusive economy: a cross-sectional study
authors: Höhn, A., Lomax, N., Rice, H., Angus, C., Brennan, A., Brown, D., Cunningham, A., Elsenbroich, C., Hughes, C., Katikireddi, S. V., McCartney, G., Seaman, R., Tsuchia, A., & Meier, P.

summary.background: Quality-adjusted life expectancy (QALE) combines length of life with health-related quality of life. But it has not been estimated at the Local Authority District scale where most policy on health inequalities is set, so the contribution of the local economy to district-level QALE has not been quantified. This paper estimated QALE for all British districts and assessed how it varies with indicators of the inclusive economy.
summary.importance: QALE is more granular than the binary healthy/unhealthy framing used by healthy life expectancy or disability-free life expectancy, because it weights years of life by continuous utility scores that capture mental and physical health together. That makes it conceptually close to the quality-adjusted life-year measure used in cost-effectiveness work, so district-level estimates can be plugged directly into economic evaluation of place-based interventions. The cross-sectional link to inclusive economy indicators gives policymakers a starting point for thinking about which dimensions of the local economy are most plausibly worth acting on, and the method transfers to other countries with comparable mortality and survey data.
summary.methods: We estimated period life tables for each Local Authority District in Great Britain for 2018 to 2020 using mid-year population estimates and death counts from the national statistical agencies, with modelled age-specific mortality rates to handle small-area imprecision. Health state utility scores at the area level were derived from the Understanding Society survey through an area-level linkage. We combined the mortality and utility components using the Sullivan method, which weights expected years of life by the prevalence of health states at each age, and reported quality-adjusted life expectancy at birth by sex with associated confidence intervals. To explore the association with economic inclusivity, we used the 13-indicator inclusive economy dataset produced by the SIPHER consortium and estimated cross-sectional associations between each indicator and quality-adjusted life expectancy at district level.
summary.findings: Quality-adjusted life expectancy varied substantially across Great Britain, with the lowest population-weighted values in Scotland and Wales and the highest in England. Variation across individual districts was wider still. Indicators of the inclusive economy together accounted for more than half of the variation in quality-adjusted life expectancy at district level. Higher inclusivity was generally associated with higher quality-adjusted life expectancy, although the direction of the association was not consistent across all 13 indicators, suggesting some residual confounding and indicator-specific issues. The estimates and the method are transferable to other national contexts where similar data are available, and they support the case for policies aimed at multiple dimensions of economic inclusion as a route to improving area-level health.

title: Evaluating the influence of taxation and social security policies on psychological distress: A microsimulation study of the UK during the COVID-19 economic crisis
authors: Kopasker, D., Bronka, P., Thomson, R. M., Khodygo, V., Kromydas, T., Meier, P., Heppenstall, A., Bambra, C., Lomax, N., Craig, P., Richiardi, M., & Katikireddi, S. V.

summary.background: Economic determinants of mental health are well established, but credible quantitative evidence on how specific taxation and social security policies translate into mental-health outcomes is scarce. Empirical evaluations are slow and constrained by ethical and practical limits on natural experiments, so few existing models can produce actionable evidence on the size and timing of policy consequences. This paper used a microsimulation framework to evaluate the UK's tax and benefit response during the COVID-19 economic crisis, comparing projections under the observed policy environment with a counterfactual in which pre-crisis policies remained in place.
summary.importance: Linking a static tax-benefit model (UKMOD) to a dynamic life-course microsimulation (SimPaths) lets analysts trace how a given fiscal package propagates through disposable income, employment and behaviour into mental-health outcomes over years. That gives Health in All Policies a quantitative engine: any tax or benefit scenario can be costed not only in fiscal terms but in projected effects on common mental disorders and on poverty. The COVID-19 application also provides a concrete case for future crisis response design, with the methodology transferable to other OECD countries with similar microsimulation infrastructure.
summary.methods: We linked two microsimulation models. UKMOD is a static tax-benefit model that calculates how a given policy environment translates gross incomes into disposable incomes for a sample of UK households drawn from the Family Resources Survey. SimPaths is a dynamic, stochastic, discrete-time microsimulation that projects life-course trajectories in income, employment and health, and embeds UKMOD so that fiscal incentives feed back into labour-supply decisions and downstream outcomes. We projected the working-age population from 2017 to 2025 under two scenarios: the observed UK policy response during COVID-19, and a counterfactual in which the pre-crisis policy environment continued unchanged. Psychological distress and the prevalence of likely cases of common mental disorders were measured using the General Health Questionnaire 12-item scale.
summary.findings: The UK policy response is estimated to have prevented a substantial fall in employment in 2020 and 2021 that would otherwise have occurred. Psychological distress rose sharply in 2020 under both scenarios, but the prevalence of likely common mental disorders rose by an additional several percentage points under the counterfactual, equivalent to around one million additional cases. Beyond 2021, as employment recovered, psychological distress returned to its pre-pandemic trend in both scenarios. The policy response also produced lasting effects on poverty, with projected poverty in 2025 lower under the observed scenario than under the counterfactual. The findings make a quantitative case that employment-protecting tax and benefit responses during an economic crisis deliver measurable mental health benefits and longer-running effects on poverty, with implications for the design of future crisis responses elsewhere.

title: Guidance on the use of complex systems models for economic evaluations of public health interventions
authors: Breeze, P. R., Squires, H., Ennis, K., Meier, P., Hayes, K., Lomax, N., Shiell, A., Kee, F., de Vocht, F., O'Flaherty, M., Gilbert, N., Purshouse, R., Robinson, S., Dodd, P. J., Strong, M., Paisley, S., Smith, R., Briggs, A., Shahab, L., Occhipinti, J.-A., Lawson, K., Bayley, T., Smith, R., Boyd, J., Kadirkamanathan, V., Cookson, R., Hernandez-Alava, M., Jackson, C. H., Karapici, A., Sassi, F., Scarborough, P., Siebert, U., Silverman, E., Vale, L., Walsh, C., & Brennan, A.

summary.background: Standard health economic models use linear and aggregate structures that suit well-bounded clinical interventions but struggle with public health interventions whose effects depend on social, environmental and behavioural feedback. Calls for greater use of complex systems methods in this area go back several years, but worked examples are few and no agreed guidance on how to do them existed, so analysts attempting such evaluations had no shared definition, design principles or selection logic. This paper convened a multidisciplinary working group to produce guidance on how complex systems models can be used for economic evaluation, including when they are needed, how they should be designed, and how the appropriate modelling technique should be chosen.
summary.importance: The guidance gives a working definition that researchers, reviewers and decision-makers can use to recognise a public health complex systems model for economic evaluation. It sets out the kinds of intervention and time horizon where these models earn their cost, makes design principles around scope, stakeholder engagement, data and validation explicit, and helps modellers choose between system dynamics, agent-based modelling and discrete-event simulation according to the question and the data available. The document gives the field a common reference for advancing complex systems economic evaluation while keeping the standards decision-makers require.
summary.methods: A multidisciplinary working group of experts in complex systems modelling and health economic evaluation was convened. The guidance was developed through a series of workshops, informed by a scoping review of the relevant literature. The group iterated on a working definition of a public health complex systems model for economic evaluation, identified principles for designing such a model, and developed advice on choosing between the principal techniques used in the field, including system dynamics, agent-based modelling and discrete-event simulation. The output is a consensus guidance paper rather than a new empirical analysis.
summary.findings: The paper proposes a definition of a public health complex systems model for economic evaluation as a quantitative, dynamic, non-linear model that incorporates feedback and interactions between elements to capture emergent outcomes and estimate health, economic and other consequences. It sets out when complex systems modelling is needed, drawing on the nature of the intervention, the feedback loops involved and the time horizons relevant to evaluation. It outlines design principles covering scope, stakeholder engagement, data and validation. And it offers practical guidance on choosing between modelling techniques, recognising that the choice is conditional on the question, the available data and the system being represented. The document supports modellers to engage with the demand for complex systems thinking in public health economic evaluation while maintaining the standards required by decision-makers.

title: DAFNI: a computational platform to support infrastructure systems research
authors: Matthews, B., Hall, J., Batty, M., Blainey, S., Cassidy, N., Choudhary, R., Coca, D., Hallett, S., Harou, J. J., James, P., Lomax, N., Oliver, P., Sivakumar, A., Tryfonas, T., & Varga, L.
journal: Proceedings of the Institution of Civil Engineers — Smart Infrastructure and Construction

summary.background: Infrastructure systems research is increasingly data-intensive and multi-disciplinary, with models combining data across energy, water, transport, digital networks and land use, and across scales from streets to nations. Individual research groups rarely have the compute, data infrastructure or sharing tools needed at that scale, and shared national compute facilities had not been built specifically for the infrastructure community, leaving modellers facing hard limits on what they can analyse and on what survives a project. This paper presents DAFNI, the Data and Analytics Facility for National Infrastructure, a national platform designed to host data, models and workflows for infrastructure systems researchers in the UK.
summary.importance: DAFNI lowers the technical barrier for any research group that wants to run national-scale, multi-sector modelling, and the containerised execution model makes models reproducible across environments. The shared data repository and access controls let teams share data and models with trusted partners under appropriate terms, addressing a long-standing barrier to collaboration in infrastructure research. By keeping data and models accessible beyond any single project, the platform supports legacy and re-use that are usually lost when a grant ends, and informs both academic and policy-facing analysis.
summary.methods: The paper describes the motivations, design and architecture of DAFNI. The platform provides high-throughput compute resources for running models at national scale, a data repository for uploading and sharing heterogeneous infrastructure datasets, and support for executing user models as containerised applications so that models can run independently of the original software environment. Models can be composed into workflows, allowing system-of-systems analysis across sectors and scales, with outputs visualised within the platform. Access control, data security and sharing arrangements are built in so that data and models can be shared with trusted partners under appropriate terms. The paper illustrates these capabilities through pilot studies.
summary.findings: DAFNI provides a single national resource that lowers the technical barriers to large-scale, cross-sector infrastructure research and supports reproducible, shareable modelling. Pilot studies show that models from different disciplines can be combined into multi-sector workflows on the platform, with the resulting outputs supporting both academic research and policy-facing analysis. By keeping data and models accessible beyond the lifetime of any single project, the platform also supports legacy and re-use, addressing one of the persistent gaps in research-software practice in this area.

title: Briefing note: A dynamic model of disposable income impacts on mental health
authors: Lomax, N., Clay, R., Archer, L., Rice, H., & Heppenstall, A.

summary.background: Household disposable income is a central lever in welfare and labour policy and is plausibly linked to mental health through several pathways, but policy evaluations rarely model these joint effects at the level of the individual. Conventional health economic evaluations don't capture how income shocks act through housing, nutrition, smoking, loneliness and neighbourhood safety simultaneously, so credible quantitative estimates of the mental-health gains from specific income-changing policies are scarce. This paper used the MINOS dynamic microsimulation model to estimate how three real policy scenarios changing household disposable income propagate into individual mental health outcomes at the population level, by sub-group and at small-area scale.
summary.importance: Modelling housing, nutrition, smoking, loneliness and neighbourhood safety as pathways between disposable income and mental health turns the income–health relationship from a single coefficient into a structure that policymakers can interrogate. The same framework lets the user swap in different policy scenarios, including ones not yet implemented, and read off both the headline effect on the working-age population and the effects on sub-groups most exposed to a given policy. The case study of Glasgow demonstrates the spatial granularity available for service-planning use.
summary.methods: MINOS is a discrete-time dynamic microsimulation that takes a longitudinal sample of UK individuals as its starting population and applies transition probability modules to each person at each step. We used Understanding Society data, including a spatially re-weighted version that allows results to be reported at small-area level in England, Wales and Scotland. The outcome is the SF-12 Mental Component Summary, a standard continuous measure of mental functioning. Five pathway modules connect household disposable income to mental health: housing quality, loneliness, neighbourhood safety, nutritional quality and smoking intensity. We modelled three scenarios: an uplift to the national living wage for low earners, a universal child benefit uplift of a fixed amount per child per week, and the introduction of the energy price cap, which for many households raises bills relative to current rates. Each scenario was run repeatedly so that mean impacts and confidence intervals could be reported.
summary.findings: Raising disposable income through either the living-wage or child-benefit scenarios produced a modest positive impact on overall mental health and a larger impact in the directly affected sub-groups. The energy price cap, by reducing disposable income for many households, produced a negative impact on overall mental health. Spatial analysis for Glasgow showed that the gains and losses are unevenly distributed across neighbourhoods, reflecting differences in the populations affected by each policy. The results support the case for treating mental-health impacts as a routine outcome in the evaluation of income policy.

title: Using e-petition data to quantify public concerns during the COVID-19 pandemic: a case study of England
authors: Clark, S. D., & Lomax, N.

summary.background: During the COVID-19 pandemic, governments had to make rapid decisions with limited insight into what their electorates wanted. Constituency-level polling was too slow and expensive to support that loop, and although previous work had used UK Parliament e-petitions to classify constituencies on broader issues, no study had focused them on COVID-19 or used them to track how concerns moved with the pandemic across the country. This paper used signatures to more than 1,500 COVID-related e-petitions in England to identify the dominant topics of public concern and to classify Westminster Parliamentary constituencies by the topics that most engaged their residents.
summary.importance: UK Parliament e-petitions are addressed directly to government, require named verified signatures and are tied to specific residential constituencies, so they offer a near-real-time, constituency-scale signal of what voters are pressing government on. A topic-modelled view of these signatures during a crisis lets analysts see which themes dominate where, and how that pattern relates to party-political divides. The approach is reusable for other crises and other countries with similar petitioning systems.
summary.methods: We assembled signatures to all UK Parliament e-petitions submitted during the COVID period that addressed pandemic-related themes, restricting analysis to constituencies in England. The text of each petition was modelled using Latent Dirichlet Allocation, an unsupervised topic-modelling approach that represents documents as mixtures of latent topics derived from word co-occurrence. The number of topics was chosen using standard model-fit metrics. We retained the topics that were coherent and substantively meaningful. For each topic we computed a measure of constituency support based on the share of signatures, and applied hierarchical clustering to group constituencies with similar topic profiles. We compared the resulting groups against general election outcomes to characterise them politically.
summary.findings: Twenty-seven coherent topics emerged from the COVID-related petition corpus, spanning health policy, schooling, business and economic support, and procedural concerns about pandemic governance. Five constituency groupings were identified. Two voted Conservative: "Middle England", concentrated in southern England, and "Equity of Support", concentrated in the Midlands and northern England, differing in the topics their residents engaged with most. Two further groups were Labour-voting, with strong engagement around education and funding issues. The fifth group bridged the political divide. The findings show that e-petition data can be used during a fast-moving crisis to map public concerns at a fine geographic scale, augmenting the more traditional sources available to policymakers and democratic institutions.

title: Infrastructure and city ontologies
authors: Varga, L., McMillan, L., Hallett, S., Russell, T., Smith, L., Truckell, I., Postnikov, A., Rodger, S., Vizcaino, N., Perkins, B., Matthews, B., & Lomax, N.
journal: Proceedings of the Institution of Civil Engineers — Smart Infrastructure and Construction

summary.background: Infrastructure and city systems generate large, heterogeneous datasets that need to be integrated across sectors and scales to address problems such as net zero, resilience and equity. Ontologies, formal representations of the concepts and relationships in a domain, are the standard tool for that integration in knowledge engineering, but each infrastructure community has developed its own, and no recent synthesis had mapped which ontologies exist, how they relate to one another, and where the gaps lie. This paper carried out a literature review of infrastructure and city ontologies and developed hypotheses about the gaps and tensions that emerge from it.
summary.importance: A mapped view of competing ontologies, and an explicit classification by level of specificity (top-level, mid-level, domain, device, applied), gives researchers a navigation tool that the previous fragmented literature did not offer. The three hypotheses set an agenda for further work: clarifying how belief systems shape non-top-level ontologies, evaluating whether a small set of top-level ontologies plus translation mechanisms outperforms continued proliferation, and articulating the role of standards in dataset adaptability and quality. Taken together, the review supports infrastructure researchers and practitioners pursuing the automation and data sharing on which integrated analysis depends.
summary.methods: We searched the academic literature for studies that define or apply ontologies in the infrastructure and city sectors, querying titles for combinations of "ontology" and sector-specific terms covering transport, energy, water, waste and telecommunications. Results were screened to focus on substantive contributions to ontology development or use, and ontologies were classified by their level of specificity, from top-level through mid-level, domain, device and applied ontologies. The review extracted recurring patterns, tensions and gaps, and the authors developed three hypotheses for further investigation.
summary.findings: The review identifies competing ontologies within each infrastructure sector and at the city level, with little explicit work on how they relate to one another or to higher-level frameworks. Three hypotheses emerge: that the belief systems underlying non-top-level ontologies can interfere with attempts at integration; that a small number of top-level ontologies together with translation mechanisms between them would do more for interoperability than continuing to proliferate domain-specific ones; and that the role of standards and information systems in shaping the adaptability and quality of datasets using ontologies needs clearer articulation. A further gap is identified in the ability of current ontologies to support automated coupling and data transformation across different scales. The review provides an agenda for ontology work that would better support integrated infrastructure and city analysis.

title: Dynamic calibration with approximate Bayesian computation for a microsimulation of disease spread
authors: Asher, M., Lomax, N., Morrissey, K., Spooner, F., & Malleson, N.

summary.background: During COVID-19, individual-based models guided major policy decisions, but their parameters were poorly known at the start and shifted as behaviour evolved. Methods for updating model parameters as new data arrive are well established in weather forecasting, but data assimilation for individual-based disease models is technically difficult and had only been demonstrated on relatively simple systems, leaving large-scale operational COVID models without a tractable way to update their parameters. This paper adapted an existing large-scale individual-based COVID-19 model and used Approximate Bayesian Computation to dynamically recalibrate its parameters as new case data arrived, testing whether this improved forecast accuracy and quantified the resulting uncertainty.
summary.importance: Approximate Bayesian Computation estimates parameter distributions by repeatedly simulating from candidate values and accepting those that produce outputs close to observed data, so unlike one-shot calibration it returns posterior distributions and not point estimates. Used in overlapping windows over a pandemic timeline, it gives modellers and policymakers both updated forecasts and a calibrated sense of how confident to be in them. The paper demonstrates the approach at a scale relevant for operational disease modelling, and is a stepping stone towards full data assimilation for individual-based models more generally.
summary.methods: We worked with the DyME individual-based COVID-19 model, which simulates a large population at individual level. We divided the pandemic timeline into a series of overlapping windows, and at each window we recalibrated the model's parameters against the most recent observed case data using Approximate Bayesian Computation, producing posterior distributions for the parameters and the resulting forecasts. The model was then used to forecast future infections, with predictions from later, better-informed windows compared against the actual observed course of the pandemic.
summary.findings: Incorporating up-to-date observations substantially improved the accuracy of infection forecasts and reduced the uncertainty around them, with later simulation windows producing markedly tighter posterior distributions. The evolution of the parameter values across windows also tracked changes in human behaviour and disease characteristics over the course of the pandemic, suggesting that dynamic recalibration captures some of the real-world structure that one-shot calibration misses. The work shows that Approximate Bayesian Computation can be used at the scale needed for realistic individual-based disease modelling, and is a useful step on the longer path towards full data assimilation for these models. The findings reinforce the case for treating forecast uncertainty as a first-class output when models inform policy.

title: Customer trends in take-away purchasing: Geospatial patterns of online food delivery platform usage in UK output areas
authors: Garcia del Toro, T., Pontin, F., Oldroyd, R., Clark, S., & Lomax, N.
journal: International Journal of Population Data Science

summary.background: The food environment has shifted with the rise of online takeaway delivery platforms, but research has focused on the physical presence of food outlets, not the digital environment that increasingly substitutes for it. Most existing work uses scraped or self-reported data that show where outlets are but not who uses them or how often, so the populations actually ordering through these platforms remain uncharacterised. This paper used transaction data from a large UK online takeaway delivery platform to map customer behaviour at small-area scale and identify the demographic correlates of average basket spend and order frequency.
summary.importance: Direct transaction records, attached to small-area geography and joined to demographic data, give a much sharper view of how people interact with the digital food environment than any other available data source. Combining these records with the Output Area Classification lets the same analysis run for any other UK area, supporting work on cuisine access, dietary inequality and the public-health consequences of takeaway-led consumption. The pipeline is reusable wherever a delivery platform can share anonymised transaction data within a secure environment.
summary.methods: We worked with a large UK online food delivery platform that provided transaction records covering anonymised customer identifiers, location information at output area level, basket detail and food outlet attributes. Data were processed within the platform's secure environment. Output areas in the UK cover roughly 125 households each. Geodemographic data came from the 2011 and 2021 Censuses, including the Output Area Classification. We characterised the geographical distribution of platform use and fitted linear regression models with median basket spend per output area as the outcome and demographic and access-related predictors as the explanatory variables. A spatial analysis focused on Leeds compared basket price, order frequency and deprivation.
summary.findings: Areas with a higher share of affluent households placed fewer orders but paid more per basket, while more deprived areas placed more orders for smaller average baskets, often for burger-type cuisine. Car ownership and the Output Area Classification supergroup were the strongest predictors of median basket spend, consistent with a joint role for deprivation and access. The Leeds analysis confirmed the pattern at fine spatial scale, with high order frequency and low basket price clustering in more deprived neighbourhoods. The work shows the value of platform transaction data for mapping the digital food environment, and suggests that cuisine availability by area is a productive direction for further work on how access shapes consumption.

title: A Dynamic Microsimulation Model for Ageing and Health in England: The English Future Elderly Model
authors: Archer, L., Lomax, N., & Tysinger, B.

summary.background: Ageing populations strain health and care systems over decades, so policy choices made today need decision-support tools that can project their long-term consequences. Existing UK health microsimulations have focused on single diseases or used static ageing methods that update populations to demographic targets at each step, and no general-purpose dynamic microsimulation for England drawing on long-running individual-level survey data had been built. This paper adapted the well-established US Future Elderly Model to England, producing the English Future Elderly Model (E-FEM): a dynamic microsimulation of the population aged 50 and over.
summary.importance: A validated dynamic microsimulation of the English population aged 50 and over equips researchers and policy partners with a reusable engine for long-horizon analysis across health and economic domains. Counterfactual scenarios that modify risk factor prevalence or transition probabilities can be run for any policy question on ageing, with outputs covering chronic disease prevalence, healthcare costs and benefit receipt together. Building on the US Future Elderly Model architecture also lets the English implementation benefit from continued international development of the underlying framework.
summary.methods: Dynamic microsimulation tracks individuals over time, applying probabilistic transitions for health states, mortality and other outcomes. We adapted the US Future Elderly Model architecture using the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing as the source of both the initial population aged 50 and over and the transition probabilities for chronic disease incidence, disability, mortality and related outcomes. The model is Markov in structure, meaning transitions at each step depend on current state. We validated outputs against external benchmarks for English life expectancy and disease prevalence, and illustrated the model's use through example counterfactual scenarios that modify input populations or transition probabilities.
summary.findings: The English Future Elderly Model reproduces observed patterns in life expectancy and chronic disease prevalence for the population aged 50 and over within acceptable bounds, supporting its use as a baseline for scenario analysis. Counterfactual experiments show how changes to risk factor prevalence or to health transitions propagate through the simulated population over time, affecting both health outcomes and related economic measures such as healthcare costs and benefit receipt. The model is positioned as a reference for subsequent work on specific policy questions in ageing, with utility for trade-off analysis across health and economic domains relevant to long-horizon decision-making.

title: Microsimulation
authors: Lomax, N.
journal: Handbook of Spatial Analysis in the Social Sciences

summary.background: Microsimulation methods model individual units such as people, households or firms over time, capturing distributional effects and behavioural heterogeneity that aggregate models miss. The field has grown substantially with better computing and microdata access, but published applications span many disciplines and use different terminology, leaving researchers without a clear introductory map. This chapter introduced microsimulation for spatial analysis, organising the methods into three strands and discussing when each is appropriate.
summary.importance: A three-strand organisation (synthetic population construction, static, dynamic) gives newcomers a structured entry point and gives experienced users a shared vocabulary across applications from population projection and tax-benefit policy to healthcare planning and small-area expenditure estimation. The chapter makes the principal trade-offs (data demand vs scenario richness, validation challenges with synthetic data) explicit, so method choice becomes a deliberate decision against the policy question rather than a path-dependent default.
summary.methods: The chapter reviews the three principal strands of microsimulation as applied in spatial contexts. The first is the construction of attribute-rich synthetic populations, where survey microdata are combined with area-level constraints (typically from census or administrative sources) so that individuals can be assigned to small geographies. The second is static microsimulation, which uses these synthetic populations to assess the immediate distributional impact of a policy change or scenario without modelling behavioural response or time. The third is dynamic microsimulation, where individuals age over time and transition between states (employed to unemployed, healthy to ill, alive to dead) according to estimated transition probabilities, supporting longer-term scenario analysis. For each strand the chapter outlines representative methods, points to widely used examples and discusses validation.
summary.findings: The three strands of microsimulation share a common motivation: capturing heterogeneity that aggregate models cannot. Each has matured to support a wide range of applications, from population projection and tax-benefit policy to healthcare planning and small-area expenditure estimation. The chapter sets out the principal trade-offs: dynamic models offer richer scenario analysis at the cost of more demanding data requirements and longer development times; synthetic populations can extend coverage but raise validation challenges since the data they produce did not previously exist. The conclusion is that microsimulation rewards careful matching of method to question, with the choice between static and dynamic approaches, and between synthetic and observed microdata, following from the policy question.

title: Objectively measuring the association between the built environment and physical activity: a systematic review and reporting framework
authors: Pontin, F. L., Jenneson, V. L., Morris, M. A., Clarke, G. P., & Lomax, N. M.
journal: International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity

summary.background: Physical inactivity is among the leading global causes of mortality, and the built environment is one of the few modifiable determinants. Objective measurement using accelerometers, GPS and geographic information systems was supposed to deliver the inter-study comparability that self-reported measures cannot, but the field still cannot pool findings because studies use different exposure definitions and report inconsistently, and no systematic review had assessed both the substantive evidence and the reporting quality together. This paper carried out a systematic review of studies that use objective measures of both the built environment and physical activity in adults, synthesised the evidence for associations between them, and developed a reporting framework to support better future research.
summary.importance: The combined evidence synthesis and the PERFORM reporting framework give researchers, reviewers and journal editors a single resource for both the substantive state of the literature and the reporting standards future work should meet. The association matrix shows where the evidence is strongest and weakest by exposure–outcome pair, and the four-area checklist (study design, built environment exposures, physical activity metrics, association analysis) translates directly into reporting requirements that would let future studies be pooled rather than tallied.
summary.methods: We followed PRISMA guidelines for a systematic search of the literature, screening titles, abstracts and full texts, and arriving at a final set of 94 studies for review. We synthesised the evidence using an association matrix that captures the direction and consistency of relationships between built environment and physical activity variables across the included studies. We then developed PERFORM (Physical and Environmental Reporting Framework for Objectively Recorded Measures), a reporting checklist covering four areas: study design, built environment exposures, physical activity metrics, and the analysis of their association. We applied the checklist to each included study to assess reporting quality.
summary.findings: Studies were geographically diverse but concentrated on a common set of exposures: walkability, access to parks and green space, and proximity-based metrics derived around home addresses. Moderate-to-vigorous physical activity was the dominant outcome, with walking the most common specific behaviour. Areas with consistent evidence for positive or negative associations were identifiable, but the reporting of participant ethnicity and socio-economic status, the justification of method choice, and the provenance of built environment data were generally weak, limiting comparability. The PERFORM checklist gives future studies a structured way to report these elements, with the aim of improving the quality and pooled use of evidence on how the built environment shapes activity behaviour.

title: Faking feature importance: A cautionary tale on the use of differentially-private synthetic data
authors: Giles, O., Hosseini, K., Mingas, G., Strickson, O., Bowler, L., Rangel Smith, C., Wilde, H., Lim, J. N., Mateen, B., Amarasinghe, K., Ghani, R., Heppenstall, A., Lomax, N., Malleson, N., O'Reilly, M., & Vollmer, S.

summary.background: Access to sensitive data is often a bottleneck for early-stage data science work, with negotiation, infrastructure and governance overheads delaying analysts before they can begin understanding their data. Differentially-private synthetic data have been proposed as a substitute, but whether they preserve the quantities analysts actually rely on at the start of a project, including which features matter most for predicting the outcome, had not been tested across realistic data settings. This paper tested whether synthetic data preserve feature importance, comparing two differentially-private methods against the originals across artificial and real-world datasets.
summary.importance: A controlled test of how feature importance survives differentially-private synthesis gives analysts in healthcare, finance and government concrete grounds for treating synthetic data as a development substrate rather than an analytical substitute. The cross-dataset evidence on where synthesis breaks down (moderate-to-high privacy, hierarchical structure, closely-ranked features) tells data owners which use-cases are safe to release and which are not, and supports a more honest framing of what synthetic data deliver.
summary.methods: We assessed how well two differentially-private synthesis methods preserve feature importance compared with the original data, across five artificially generated datasets designed to expose different difficulty regimes and three real-world datasets (US Census-derived adult income, Costa Rican household poverty, and a Polish quality of life survey). For each dataset, we generated synthetic versions at a range of privacy levels, computed feature importance from the original and synthetic data using standard model-agnostic measures, and quantified agreement using utility scores that capture similarity of ranked importance and predictive performance. Independent column resampling served as a naive baseline.
summary.findings: Synthetic data did not produce accurate representations of feature importance when privacy was set to moderate or high levels, with low mean similarity to the original data and large run-to-run variance. Performance improved when privacy was loosened or when the data structure was simple, particularly when truly important features were well separated from less important ones. In the more nuanced real-world settings, synthetic data sometimes reranked features in ways that would alter modelling decisions, and in hierarchical data the synthesis methods failed to capture structure. Differentially-private synthetic data are not currently a safe substitute for the original at the exploratory phase, and analysts using them should expect to revisit feature decisions once the real data become available.

title: Internal migration: census data as a gold standard for insight and visualisation
authors: Lomax, N.

summary.background: Internal migration reshapes the size and composition of local populations, and the UK census is the only source that asks the whole population about its migration. But long-term comparisons across UK censuses are obstructed by changing boundaries, by under-enumeration adjustments and by the way "origin unstated" responses were handled in earlier years, leaving the long-run dynamics hard to see at small-area scale. This paper used data from the 1981, 1991, 2001 and 2011 censuses to map how internal migration propensity and efficiency have changed across the UK over four decades.
summary.importance: A harmonised, decade-by-decade series of LAD-level migration rates and efficiency ratios gives migration researchers, demographers and policy analysts a visual reference for the long-run dynamics of UK internal migration at a consistent small-area scale. The documented boundary, enumeration and "origin unstated" adjustments make the series reusable for later studies, and provide a clear baseline against which 2021 Census data can be incorporated once it is available for all four UK nations.
summary.methods: I used the Special Migration Statistics from the 1981, 1991, 2001 and 2011 UK censuses, with established adjustments to reallocate "origin unstated" migrants in 1981 and 2001 and to correct for disclosure-control under-enumeration in 1991. Local Authority Districts were harmonised to consistent boundaries across decades. Northern Ireland was excluded from the first two periods owing to data unavailability. Two summary measures were calculated for each area and decade: a net migration rate per thousand population, and a migration efficiency ratio capturing the balance between inflows and outflows as a share of total turnover. Results were presented at LAD scale and aggregated to a City Region typology built around 13 UK Core Cities.
summary.findings: Across the four decades, both the net migration rate at City Region scale and the migration efficiency ratio at LAD scale declined, consistent with the well-documented long-run fall in UK internal migration propensity. The spatial pattern shifted: urban Core zones lost population through net migration in 1981 and 1991, with a partial reversal by 2001 and clear re-urbanisation by 2011. Migration also became less efficient as a redistributor of population, with both strongly gaining and strongly losing areas becoming rarer. The maps provide a visual reference for these long-run shifts at a consistent spatial scale, and the documented adjustments offer a baseline for incorporating 2021 Census data once it is available across all UK nations.

title: A foresight whole systems obesity classification for the English UK biobank cohort
authors: Clark, S., Lomax, N., Birkin, M., & Morris, M.

summary.background: Obesity is shaped by social, economic, biological, behavioural and environmental drivers acting together. The 2007 UK Foresight obesity system map set this out, but most quantitative research still isolates single exposures, and no published study had operationalised the systems map as a multi-domain classification of individuals, leaving policy makers planning whole-system interventions without a way to identify the groups most exposed to the system as a whole. This paper built a whole-systems obesity classification of UK Biobank participants drawing on the Foresight domains, and tested whether the resulting groups discriminate between weight statuses.
summary.importance: Eight named, recognisable groups distinguished by combined exposure to obesity drivers (and not just any single one) give public-health teams a vocabulary for designing and targeting whole-system interventions, and a stratification within which to read disparate single-variable effects. The Foresight-aligned domain structure means the variables can be reassembled for other cohorts where similar measures are available, supporting comparable classifications outside UK Biobank.
summary.methods: Using the UK Biobank cohort of adults aged 40 to 70 recruited in England, Scotland and Wales, we selected variables that map onto the five Foresight domains: societal influences, individual psychology, individual physiology, individual physical activity, and physical activity environment. We applied k-means clustering, an unsupervised method that groups individuals with similar profiles across the selected variables, with the number of clusters chosen by standard diagnostics. To assess whether the classification predicted weight status, we used multinomial logistic regression, which estimates the relative risk of being overweight or having obesity across the resulting groups, with healthy-weight participants as the reference. Each group was described through pen portraits drawn from its variable profile.
summary.findings: Eight distinct groups emerged from the classification, labelled to reflect their dominant characteristics, including "Younger, urban hard-pressed", "Comfortable, fit families", "Active manual workers" and "Deprived with less healthy lifestyles". The "Comfortable, fit families" group had a higher proportion of healthy-weight participants than the others. Three groups, "Active manual workers", "Stressed and not in work" and "Deprived with less healthy lifestyles", carried increased relative risk of overweight or obesity. The classification distinguishes groups of individuals who differ both in their exposure to known obesity drivers and in their weight outcomes, supporting its use as a tool for designing and targeting whole-system interventions across populations beyond Biobank where similar variables can be assembled.

title: An Open-Source Model for Projecting Small Area Demographic and Land-Use Change
authors: Lomax, N., Smith, A. P., Archer, L., Ford, A., & Virgo, J.

summary.background: Infrastructure investments in transport, energy, water and digital networks depend on detailed projections of where people will live and what households will look like. But official UK projections are produced at coarse Local Authority scale and as pre-tabulated outputs that cannot easily be adapted for scenario analysis, and no open, adaptable framework that combines demographic projection with land-use allocation at fine spatial scale existed for the whole UK. This paper developed such a framework as open-source software, and used a UK case study to demonstrate its application for infrastructure scenario testing.
summary.importance: Open-source software lowers the entry cost for any infrastructure modelling team or academic user that wants fine-scale demographic and household inputs, and the coupling to a land-use model lets the same framework move from people to where they live to what infrastructure they need. The models serve as the demographic engine of the National Infrastructure Systems Model and adapt to local data and assumptions in other contexts, supporting reproducible scenario analysis at a resolution national statistical agencies do not publish.
