summary.methods: The framework comprises a cohort-component demographic projection at small-area scale, a household projection that translates the demographic outputs into household formation by type and tenure, and a land-use model that allocates the projected population spatially according to development constraints and policies. Demographic projection uses standard inputs of fertility, mortality and internal and international migration, calibrated to national statistical agency outputs and adjustable for scenario analysis. The framework is implemented as open-source software so other teams can adapt it to local data and assumptions. We applied it to the Cambridge to Milton Keynes to Oxford development arc as a case study, illustrating how scenarios of housing-led growth and economic shocks propagate through to fine-scale population and land-use outcomes.
summary.findings: The framework produces high-resolution demographic and household projections that align with national statistical agency outputs at coarser scales while supporting alternative scenarios at the small-area level. In the case study, the housing-led growth scenarios produced markedly different spatial patterns of population from the baseline, with corresponding implications for the demand for infrastructure across transport, water, energy and digital sectors. The models serve as the demographic engine of the National Infrastructure Systems Model and provide a reusable foundation for projects where bespoke, fine-scale demographic inputs are needed but not currently feasible to develop from scratch.

title: A synthetic population dataset for estimating small area health and socio-economic outcomes in Great Britain
authors: Wu, G., Heppenstall, A., Meier, P., Purshouse, R., & Lomax, N.

summary.background: Modelling health, economic and social outcomes for sub-groups and small areas needs individual-level data with rich attributes, but real microdata are restricted to secure settings or coarse geographies. Spatial microsimulation produces synthetic individuals at fine spatial scale, but no publicly documented, attribute-rich synthetic population existed for the whole of Great Britain, so researchers needing one had to build it from scratch each time. This paper constructed a synthetic micro dataset for Great Britain with detailed attributes derived from census, survey and administrative sources, and documented its construction and validation.
summary.importance: A re-usable synthetic population removes the duplicated effort that has dogged microsimulation work in Great Britain, and the documented validation against known totals and external reference data makes the dataset trustworthy as a baseline input. The same synthetic population already feeds the SIPHER consortium's dynamic microsimulation and agent-based modelling of inclusive-economy policy, and the methodology is transferable: other research teams can adopt it directly or extend it with additional attributes for their own small-area analyses of health and socio-economic outcomes.
summary.methods: We constructed the synthetic population through spatial microsimulation, combining individual-level attributes from the Understanding Society survey with population totals from the 2011 UK Census and mid-year population estimates. The Census provides a complete population base with limited attributes; the survey is attribute-rich for a sample; spatial microsimulation reconciles the two by assigning survey individuals to small geographies in proportions that match the census constraints. The output is a set of individuals each carrying demographic, socio-economic and other attributes and located within a defined geographical zone in Great Britain. We validated the synthetic population by comparing aggregate distributions of attributes against known totals and by examining attribute distributions for selected sub-populations and areas, including Greater Manchester, Sheffield, Glasgow and Cardiff.
summary.findings: The synthetic population reproduces the constraining totals from the Census and mid-year estimates well, with attribute distributions for the example sub-populations and geographies consistent with observed patterns from external sources. The dataset can be aggregated, cross-tabulated and augmented with further data, and it serves as the input population for the SIPHER consortium's dynamic microsimulation and agent-based modelling work on inclusive economy policy. By making the construction and validation transparent, the paper enables other teams to adapt the dataset for their own analyses of small-area health and socio-economic outcomes across Great Britain.

title: Targeted policy intervention for reducing red meat consumption: conflicts and trade-offs
authors: James, W. H. M., Lomax, N., Birkin, M., & Collins, L. M.

summary.background: Universal limits on red and processed meat consumption are proposed to address both cancer risk and climate change, but the secondary consequences for nutrient intake, the meat industry and individual diets are typically considered in isolation. Dietary policies are treated in silos and universal limits are blunt instruments, yet targeted policy intervention has been used in alcohol and tobacco control without being systematically applied to red meat. This paper used UK dietary survey data to identify the demographic groups whose consumption exceeds World Cancer Research Fund recommendations and modelled the impact of adherence on nutrient intake, greenhouse gas emissions and the meat industry.
summary.importance: The framework quantifies several trade-offs that dietary policy currently treats one at a time: lowering meat intake cuts cancer risk and greenhouse gas emissions but also drops intake of nutrients (iron, zinc, vitamins B12 and B3) for which red meat is a major source. Quantifying them jointly lets policymakers see where harms can offset gains, and the focus on high-consuming sub-groups gives a template for intervention design that protects low consumers and concentrates effort where reduction would have most effect. The approach is extensible to other dietary policies that face similar tensions.
summary.methods: We used food diary records from over 5,000 individuals in the UK National Diet and Nutrition Survey, with consumption disaggregated to specific products. We compared individual intake against the World Cancer Research Fund guidelines for red and processed red meat to identify demographic groups most likely to exceed the recommendations. We then synthetically modified the food diary data to simulate universal adherence to the guidelines and quantified the resulting changes in total consumption, intake of nutrients commonly obtained from red meat (iron, zinc, vitamin B12, vitamin B3), fat and saturated fat intake, and global warming potential. We projected the impacts forward under alternative population scenarios and assessed how the picture would shift once meat substitutes were introduced.
summary.findings: Excess consumption was concentrated in identifiable demographic groups, supporting a case for targeted intervention at those groups. Adherence reduced overall red and processed red meat consumption and greenhouse gas emissions from the diet, with corresponding falls in fat and saturated fat intake. Intake of iron, zinc and other nutrients commonly obtained from red meat fell as well, raising the possibility of nutritional shortfalls in groups whose baseline intake of these nutrients was already low. The introduction of meat substitutes can offset some of these effects, but the direction depends on the substitute. The framework gives policymakers a way to model the joint health, environmental and industrial consequences of red meat policies and to design interventions that minimise harmful trade-offs.

title: A worlds-eye view of the United Kingdom through parliamentary e-petitions
authors: Clark, S. D., & Lomax, N.
journal: The British Journal of Politics and International Relations

summary.background: The UK diaspora is large, and active proposals would extend its UK voting rights beyond the current 15-year cap. Survey-based approaches to diaspora politics are expensive and patchy, and the existing UK e-petition literature has focused on domestic constituencies, leaving the international signal in the data untouched. This paper used signatures to UK Parliament e-petitions from people resident abroad to map the political concerns of the UK diaspora and to identify groupings of countries and territories whose concerns are similar.
summary.importance: E-petition signatures carry verified country information, so they offer a cheap, repeatable indicator of which UK political topics generate engagement among Britons abroad. UK political parties are starting to mobilise these voters, and a country-level classification of diaspora concerns gives them an empirical basis for tailored outreach. The method generalises to other legislatures with petitioning systems and to other questions about how diaspora attention tracks events back home.
summary.methods: We used signatures to UK Parliament e-petitions debated between 2017 and 2019, retaining those associated with countries and territories outside the UK. Petition text was modelled using Latent Dirichlet Allocation, an unsupervised topic-modelling approach that represents documents as mixtures of latent topics derived from word co-occurrence. We chose the number of topics using standard model-fit metrics. Each petition was assigned to its most probable topic, and topics were curated into broader thematic collections. We then summarised the share of signatures each topic attracted in each country, territory or region, and applied hierarchical clustering to identify groups of locations with similar topic profiles. We compared each group's emphasis against the UK signature pattern to identify where the diaspora aligns with or departs from domestic concerns.
summary.findings: Sixty distinct topics were identified across the petition corpus, covering crime, education, environment, finance, health, international relations, politics, society, transport and a miscellaneous residual. Five meaningful country groupings emerged, differing in the topics that attracted the most diaspora engagement. Brexit-related concerns were the most popular topic in nearly every country and territory, with public scrutiny of UK politics and UK devolution also widely shared. Some groups departed sharply from the UK pattern, with migrant rights and citizenship topping the agenda in Hong Kong and family or childcare topics in Poland. The five-group classification gives UK political parties an empirical basis for tailoring outreach to expatriate communities whose concerns are distinct, and suggests that diaspora engagement should be treated as differentiated by location.

title: Contemporary Applications For Spatially Integrated Social Science
authors: Corcoran, J., Lomax, N., & Lombard, J.

summary.background: The spatial turn in the social sciences has accelerated over the past two decades, with applications spanning quantitative and qualitative methods and a wide range of substantive areas. But few collections bring the international scholarship together in one place, so readers lack a curated view of how the field is being applied today. This editorial introduced a special issue gathering recent international research on spatially integrated social science, drawn from the Applied Geography Commission of the International Geographical Union.
summary.importance: The collection illustrates the contemporary range of spatially integrated social science (from urban patenting and innovation through mobility, housing, planning and demographic change), giving readers a single curated view of where the field is being applied. By bringing together work from across the International Geographical Union's Applied Geography Commission, the special issue also signals the international scope of these approaches and provides a starting point for researchers and policymakers looking to identify methods and partners for their own substantive questions.
summary.methods: The editorial accompanies a special issue of *Applied Spatial Analysis and Policy*. The papers were drawn from recent meetings of the Applied Geography Commission and span topics including the geography of urban innovation, urban mobility, transport, planning and housing. The editorial introduces each paper, sets out its contribution and locates it within the wider spatially integrated social science agenda.
summary.findings: The collection illustrates the range of contemporary applications of spatial analysis in the social sciences, from regression-based studies of urban patenting and human capital, to mobility studies using anonymised vehicle data, to research on housing, planning and demographic change. Taken together the papers argue that spatially integrated approaches have moved well past their late-1990s origins and are now indispensable to addressing many of the challenges facing people and places.

title: Clustering Accelerometer Activity Patterns from the UK Biobank Cohort
authors: Clark, S., Lomax, N., Morris, M., Pontin, F., & Birkin, M.

summary.background: Wrist-worn accelerometers capture rich, continuous records of physical activity, but published analyses usually reduce these to averages or threshold-based counts that throw away the shape of the activity profile. Summary measures miss when in the week activity occurs and how it is distributed across days, leaving studies of activity and health outcomes reliant on coarse measures that may obscure relationships with sociodemographic factors and disease. This paper developed a clustering of whole-week activity profiles from the UK Biobank cohort to identify distinct activity types and assess how they relate to socio-demographic, socioeconomic and health characteristics.
summary.importance: A typology of whole-week activity profiles gives public-health researchers and surveillance teams a way to study activity as a shape, not a scalar, with clusters differentiated by sociodemographic, socioeconomic, health and circadian characteristics. The named clusters (Active 9 to 5, Live for the Weekend, Sedate, and so on) become candidate exposures for downstream health studies such as body mass index or COVID-19 severity. By returning the clusters to UK Biobank, the paper makes them available to other researchers without each team having to redo the clustering.
summary.methods: We applied k-medoids clustering, a partitioning method that uses real observations as cluster centres and is less sensitive to outliers than k-means, to over 90,000 weekly accelerometer profiles from UK Biobank participants. Each profile captured the timing and intensity of activity through the week. The resulting clusters were characterised using the socio-demographic, socioeconomic, health and circadian rhythm data also collected by UK Biobank, so that the activity types could be related to person-level characteristics.
summary.findings: Nine distinct activity profiles emerged from the data, capturing both the timing of activity across the week and its intensity: Active 9 to 5, Active, Morning Movers, Get up and Active, Live for the Weekend, Moderates, Leisurely 9 to 5, Sedate, and Inactive. The clusters were clearly differentiated by sociodemographic, socioeconomic and health characteristics, and by circadian rhythm. The typology is intended to complement existing summary measures and to support studies of how activity relates to outcomes such as body mass index or COVID-19 severity. The clusters have been returned to UK Biobank for use by other researchers.

title: Defining distance thresholds for migration research
authors: Lomax, N., Norman, P., & Darlington-Pollock, F.

summary.background: Migration studies routinely impose a distance cut-off to distinguish "short" from "long" moves or "residential mobility" from "internal migration". But the cut-off is often arbitrary or driven by administrative boundaries, and without evidence on how sensitive findings are to that choice, researchers have had little basis for choosing one threshold over another. This paper tested how the choice of threshold affects estimates of how population characteristics relate to migration propensity.
summary.importance: Quantifying how migration findings shift across 16 distance thresholds gives migration researchers a concrete demonstration of the sensitivity their study design is exposed to. It supports a stronger reporting standard, with threshold choice justified rather than inherited from data conventions, and it shows reviewers and meta-analysts where studies that differ only in cut-off are likely to be incomparable. The same sensitivity analysis can be re-run in any other country with comparable individual-level census data.
summary.methods: We used the 2011 Census Sample of Anonymised Records for England and Wales. We fitted binary logistic regression models of the probability of having moved in the year before the census, with population characteristics including age, sex, qualifications, occupation, ethnicity and family status as predictors. We repeated the analysis using 16 different distance thresholds for what counts as a "migration", and compared the size, direction and significance of estimated effects across the thresholds.
summary.findings: The estimated odds of migrating, and the apparent relationship between population characteristics and migration propensity, varied substantially across the 16 distance thresholds. Some predictors that were significant at one threshold were not at another, and effect sizes shifted with threshold choice. The findings argue that distance cut-offs in migration research should be chosen deliberately for the population and the research question, and that the threshold choice should be reported and justified as part of study design.

title: A dynamic microsimulation model for epidemics
authors: Spooner, F., Abrams, J. F., Morrissey, K., Shaddick, G., Batty, M., Milton, R., Dennett, A., Lomax, N., Malleson, N., Nelissen, N., Coleman, A., Nur, J., Jin, Y., Greig, R., Shenton, C., & Birkin, M.

summary.background: COVID-19 outcomes and the policies introduced to contain them have been distributed unevenly across communities, in ways that depend on what people do day-to-day. Aggregate compartmental models cannot represent the activity patterns, contact structures and socio-demographic heterogeneity that drove unequal outcomes, so policy assessment using them risks missing how interventions land in different places. This paper introduced a dynamic microsimulation framework that links individual daily activities to COVID-19 transmission and used it to assess intervention scenarios.
summary.importance: Linking a fine-resolution synthetic population to activity-based contact patterns gives epidemic modelling an area-level engine that aggregate SEIR cannot match. The framework supports counterfactual policy analysis at country or county scale within computationally feasible limits, with explicit treatment of who interacts with whom and where. That makes it directly usable for evaluating place-based interventions, and the approach extends beyond COVID to any disease whose transmission is shaped by daily activity patterns.
summary.methods: We built a data-driven framework that combines microsimulation, a synthetic population at fine spatial resolution, and a representation of disease transmission on activity-based contact patterns. The framework was designed to be computationally efficient enough to run at country or county scale. We illustrated its capabilities by applying it to Devon during the first wave of the pandemic in the UK, comparing simulated outcomes under the actual lockdown timing with scenarios in which lockdown was introduced earlier.
summary.findings: Within the case study, an earlier introduction of lockdown was estimated to lower the peak number of COVID-19 cases and to reduce overall infections during the initial outbreak by close to half. The wider contribution is methodological: the framework supports area-level assessment of interventions with explicit treatment of activity-based contacts and population heterogeneity, and is computationally tractable. The paper argues that this style of dynamic, spatially detailed microsimulation will be necessary for understanding how interventions land in different places and on different populations.

title: On the Use of 'Glyphmaps' for Analysing the Scale and Temporal Spread of COVID-19 Reported Cases
authors: Beecham, R., Dykes, J., Hama, L., & Lomax, N.

summary.background: Visualising area-level COVID-19 case data forces a trade-off between showing the trajectory of the outbreak and keeping its geographic context. Most early-pandemic visualisations were snapshot maps that lost time, national time-series that lost place, or animations that depended on visual memory across frames, and the design space for static graphics combining time and place had not been systematically explored for pandemic data. This paper developed and evaluated a set of glyphmap designs that place small time-series charts at each Local Authority's geographic location and assessed how well each supports analytical questions about the scale and temporal spread of the virus across England.
summary.importance: A framework of Data Requirements and Design Requirements turns ad hoc glyphmap design into a checklist that analysts and communicators can apply when visualising area-level disease data. The evaluation across timing, magnitude and synchrony aspects of the spread helps users match design choice to the question they are trying to answer, while the documented trade-offs (clutter, occlusion, salience bias) flag where each design will mislead. The provided code makes the designs immediately reusable for other countries and other phenomena where time and place both matter.
summary.methods: We developed several glyphmap designs for COVID case data at the Local Authority scale in England, in which a small chart for each area is placed at the area's geographic location. We then derived a framework of Data Requirements and Design Requirements from existing visualisation attempts and from analytical questions about the outbreak, and used the framework to evaluate the designs. The evaluation was supported by an observational data analysis using each design in turn.
summary.findings: Each design exposes different aspects of the spread, including the timing of peaks across areas, the relative magnitude of cases, and the synchrony of trajectories between neighbouring areas. The framework makes the design-decision space explicit, allowing analysts to choose a glyphmap whose strengths match their question. The paper also identifies the trade-offs inherent in any such design, including clutter, occlusion and salience bias, and provides code so that the designs can be applied to other countries and to phenomena beyond the pandemic.

title: Estimating household mobility using novel Big Data
authors: Lomax, N.
journal: Big Data Applications in Geography and Planning

summary.background: Internal moves account for more population redistribution at local level in the UK than international migration does. But the data underpinning official annual estimates rely on administrative systems not designed to measure migration, with known under- and over-counts in particular demographic groups, and commercial big-data alternatives had not been systematically assessed against the official figures. This chapter used a big-data source on household moves derived from the Royal Mail postal forwarding service, combined with online property data, to estimate household mobility and compared the result with official estimates and with census flows.
summary.importance: Combining forwarding-service records with property attributes gives statistical agencies and demographers a new piece of evidence to set alongside official estimates, and reveals movements the official administrative estimates appear to under-count. The chapter's explicit treatment of representativeness, by property type and area characteristics, sets a template for how commercial big-data sources should be appraised before they enter routine use, supporting a tiered mobility evidence base that combines big data with administrative and census sources.
summary.methods: The chapter draws on Royal Mail postal forwarding records, which capture households who have requested mail be redirected to a new address, combined with property attributes from an online property search portal. We estimated mobility patterns by property type and by area characteristics, then compared the resulting estimates with the most recent UK census mobility data and with the annual administrative estimates produced by ONS, NRS and NISRA. We discussed how coverage of the forwarding service affects representativeness and what the comparisons imply for data quality.
summary.findings: The forwarding-service-plus-property big data captured spatial and household-type patterns broadly consistent with the census, and revealed some movements that the official administrative estimates appear to under-count. The data are richest where forwarding-service take-up is highest, which is itself patterned by household type and tenure, so they sit alongside official sources as a complement. The chapter argues that big data sources of this kind can sit alongside administrative and census data in a tiered system of mobility evidence, and identifies the validation and bias questions that further work needs to address before they enter routine use.

title: Can a data driven obesity classification system identify those at risk of severe COVID-19 in the UK Biobank cohort study?
authors: Clark, S., Morris, M., Lomax, N., & Birkin, M.

summary.background: Severe COVID-19 outcomes have been associated with obesity, but no single weight or sociodemographic variable captures the multi-dimensional risk profile of an individual. COVID risk research typically isolates one risk factor at a time, and whether a classification that groups people by combined obesity-related profile would carry useful information about a downstream outcome like COVID had not been tested. This paper tested whether a previously developed obesity classification of UK Biobank participants, built around the Foresight obesity systems map, identified meaningful differences in COVID-19 outcomes.
summary.importance: Multi-dimensional risk classifications make combined profiles legible to clinicians and the public in a way single-variable regressions cannot, and the obesity classes turn out to differentiate COVID-19 testing, infection, hospitalisation and mortality in interpretable ways. That makes the framework usable for risk stratification, for designing public health messaging and for downstream studies of long COVID. The same Biobank-trained classification supports re-use across other health outcomes that share obesity-adjacent risk factors.
summary.methods: We used a previously published k-means classification of UK Biobank participants based on 52 variables grouped into 23 classification dimensions, informed by the Foresight obesity systems map covering food production and consumption, societal influences, psychology, activity, environment and biology. The resulting seven classes ranged from active workers to retirees with healthy lifestyles, stressed and not in work, deprived with less-healthy lifestyles, and comfortable professionals and families. We tested whether class membership was associated with four COVID-19 outcomes: being tested, testing positive, hospital admission, and death.
summary.findings: The obesity classification identified meaningful differentials across the four COVID-19 outcomes. Some classes had higher rates of testing and positive tests; others had elevated hospitalisation and mortality, with patterns consistent with the underlying socioeconomic, ethnic and health profiles of the classes. The paper argues that multi-dimensional classifications of this kind are useful complements to single-variable analyses for identifying and prioritising COVID risk and for studying determinants of long COVID, because they capture combinations of risk factors that single-variable models can obscure.

title: Privacy-preserving data publishing through anonymization, statistical disclosure control, and de-identification
authors: Loukides, G., & Lomax, N.

summary.background: Datasets describing individuals are increasingly valuable for research and policy, but also carry real risks of disclosure and misuse. Legal frameworks require protection and public trust depends on it, yet the privacy literature is fragmented across communities and assumes a methodological background that many researchers don't have, leaving them without an accessible map of available techniques. This chapter provided a methodological overview of anonymization and statistical disclosure control techniques aimed at researchers and practitioners working with personal data.
summary.importance: Organising techniques by data type (microdata, tabular, set-valued, relational) gives researchers and practitioners a structured way to pick methods appropriate to their data, with the underlying threat models and the privacy–utility trade-off made explicit. Coverage of open-source implementations turns the review into something operational. The chapter argues for privacy protection across the full data lifecycle, giving data owners and analysts a basis for designing release pipelines that fit both their data and the legal framework they operate under.
summary.methods: The chapter reviewed the main technical approaches for privacy-preserving data publishing, organised by data type. Methods covered included k-anonymity and related frameworks for microdata, statistical disclosure control techniques for tabular data, anonymization for set-valued data (such as purchase or location histories), and methods for data with both relational and set-valued attributes. We also reviewed open-source software implementations of the main algorithms.
summary.findings: The chapter provides a structured map of the available privacy-preserving techniques and their appropriate application. It distinguishes the assumptions and threat models behind different methods, the kinds of data each method handles best, and the trade-offs between privacy guarantee and utility of the released data. The work argues that privacy protection must be designed across the full data lifecycle, from collection through sharing to public release, and that the right combination of techniques depends on the data type, the user community and the legal framework.

title: Socio-demographic determinants of physical activity and app usage from smartphone data
authors: Pontin, F., Lomax, N., Clarke, G., & Morris, M. A.

summary.background: Smartphone-based activity apps generate large secondary datasets at low cost, offering scale and continuity that surveys and small wearable studies cannot match. But their use is selective, and the sociodemographic bias this introduces had not been characterised, so secondary data from these sources cannot be safely used to draw population-level inferences. This paper used data from a commercial activity app in the UK to characterise both the physical activity it captured and the sociodemographic profile of its users.
summary.importance: Quantifying the sociodemographic profile of smartphone activity-app users and their activity patterns tells public-health researchers and behavioural analysts how far inferences from app data generalise, and where they need correction. The weekly and seasonal patterns the data reveal at scale also extend what wearable studies of similar phenomena can show, complementing them rather than competing. The framework is reusable for assessing other commercial wellbeing or activity datasets before they enter substantive analysis.
summary.methods: We used data from a commercial app designed to incentivise physical activity in the UK. We linked app users to area-level sociodemographic information to characterise their profile, and analysed daily, weekly and seasonal patterns of activity captured by the app. We then assessed how the proportion of users meeting WHO physical activity guidelines varied by sex, age and area socioeconomic status.
summary.findings: App users were disproportionately female, aged 25 to 50, and living in areas with a higher proportion of lower-socioeconomic-status residents. Longer-term app use rose with age. More male users met the WHO guideline activity threshold, even though female users recorded longer daily activity duration on average. Clear weekly and seasonal trends were visible in the activity data. The findings argue that smartphone activity data can illuminate physical activity behaviour at population scale but that the selectivity of who uses such apps has to be accounted for when interpreting what the data show.

title: Characterisation of Temporal Patterns in Step Count Behaviour from Smartphone App Data: An Unsupervised Machine Learning Approach
authors: Pontin, F., Lomax, N., Clarke, G., & Morris, M. A.
journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health

summary.background: Smartphone step count data record physical activity continuously for many users over months or years. But the bulk of analysis still reduces these to aggregate measures such as average daily steps, hiding how activity is distributed across days and seasons and how short-term routines feed into longer-term patterns. This paper applied unsupervised machine learning to identify distinct weekly and seasonal patterns of step-count behaviour from smartphone app data, and characterised how those patterns relate to user demographics and activity type.
summary.importance: Separate weekly and seasonal clusterings give public-health researchers and behavioural scientists structured ways to characterise habitual activity that aggregate measures cannot reach. The linkage between weekly and seasonal cluster membership shows how short-term routines feed into longer-term patterns, with clear implications for intervention design (whether to target a routine, a season or both). The approach is reusable on other smartphone or wearable datasets that share the same temporal granularity.
summary.methods: We applied k-means and agglomerative hierarchical clustering to smartphone app step count data, separately at the level of weekly profiles and yearlong seasonal profiles. We then characterised each cluster by the demographic profile of its users and by the activity types most commonly recorded within it. We examined links between weekly clusters and seasonal clusters to assess how short-term routines build into longer-term patterns.
summary.findings: Seven seasonal clusters emerged, all of which showed elevated activity during summer months and a clear response to daylight saving. Six weekly clusters showed contrasting weekday-versus-weekend balances that produced different probabilities of meeting physical activity guidelines. Cluster membership was strongly associated with sex and age, and with the type of activity users preferred. Weekly cluster membership was linked to seasonal cluster membership, showing how short-term routines contribute to longer-term activity profiles. The paper argues that unsupervised methods applied to smartphone data offer a way to move beyond aggregate measures of physical activity and toward an account of habitual behaviour that respects its temporal structure.

title: Data linkage and its applications for planning support systems
authors: Birkin, M., James, W., Lomax, N., & Smith, A.

summary.background: Big data have opened new possibilities for planning support systems, but realising them depends on linking diverse sources to a coherent representation of the population being planned for. Planning support has traditionally drawn on aggregate area data, which limits the questions it can answer, and the role of linkage and spatial microsimulation as a route to richer representations had been under-discussed in the planning literature. This chapter set out a framework for combining demographic, economic and social data through spatial microsimulation, and showed how the linked outputs can feed planning support systems.
summary.importance: Spatial microsimulation as an integration layer lets planners attach attributes from many sources to a single synthetic population, opening up planning support to questions that aggregate area data cannot answer. The infrastructure case study shows the same framework working at very long horizons; the pork-demand case study shows it absorbing domain-specific attitudinal and environmental data. The chapter also flags the calibration, public-acceptance and access questions that come with linked individual-level data, giving planners a realistic view of the practical and ethical bar to clear.
summary.methods: The chapter set out the conceptual framework for using spatial microsimulation to combine demographic, economic and social datasets at fine spatial resolution, and to feed the resulting linked data into planning support systems. We illustrated the framework with two case studies in different planning contexts: a national infrastructure modelling system requiring socio-economic demand data over very long time horizons, and a study of UK pork product demand linking demographic data with expenditure, lifestyle, dietary, attitudinal and environmental information.
summary.findings: Both case studies show that spatial microsimulation can serve as an integration layer for planning support systems, attaching attributes from many sources to a common synthetic population. The infrastructure example demonstrates that the same framework can serve very long planning horizons; the pork demand example shows it can integrate domain-specific attitudinal and environmental data. The chapter closes with directions for further work, including stronger calibration and validation, extension into health and social policy, and the public-acceptance, legal and access questions that linked individual-level data raise.

title: Geodemographic Patterns of Meat Expenditure in Great Britain
authors: James, W. H. M., Lomax, N., Birkin, M., & Collins, L. M.

summary.background: Meat consumption sits at the intersection of public health, environmental impact and the economics of the food system. Published UK expenditure data are at regional scale and do not differentiate the sociodemographic groups driving the patterns, and little work has combined geodemographic classification with detailed meat expenditure, even though the public-health and environmental cases for change rest on knowing which groups consume which products. This paper used a geodemographic classification combined with small-area expenditure estimates to examine spatial and temporal patterns of meat expenditure across Great Britain between 2008 and 2017.
summary.importance: A meat-specific geodemographic view shows which areas and groups drive consumption of which categories, and how that profile shifts over time. That gives meat-industry policymakers, public-health bodies and environmental analysts a common picture to argue from, and supports targeted intervention design (where price, environmental attitudes or cultural and religious considerations are most relevant). The framework can be re-run as new expenditure estimates arrive and adapts to other consumption domains where similar small-area inputs exist.
summary.methods: We drew on previously produced local-authority-level expenditure estimates for meat categories built using spatial microsimulation, and constructed a geodemographic classification of areas based on their meat expenditure profile across categories. We then examined how the proportion of expenditure on different meat categories varied across these geodemographic groups, and how those patterns changed across the period.
summary.findings: Some meat categories, such as sausages, showed relatively stable expenditure patterns across the period, while others, such as lamb, showed a falling share of total meat expenditure and rising inequality of purchasing across areas. Short-term changes in some categories could plausibly be attributed to price variability, demand elasticities or disease scares. Differences between geodemographic groups were consistent with the influence of environmental attitudes, financial constraints and the presence of communities who do not eat particular meats for religious or cultural reasons. The findings argue for fine-scale, geodemographically aware approaches to monitoring food consumption, and offer a tool for policymakers in the meat industry and adjacent domains.

title: On the use of 'glyphmaps' for analysing Covid-19 reported cases
authors: Beecham, R., Dykes, J., Hama, L., & Lomax, N.

summary.background: Visualising Covid-19 case data at small-area level forces a trade-off between showing the trajectory of the outbreak over time and keeping geographic context. Most published case visualisations are either snapshot maps that lose the time dimension or national time-series charts that lose the geographic one, and static designs that combine the two have not been systematically explored, leaving design choices ad hoc. This paper developed and evaluated a set of glyphmap designs that arrange small time-series charts in geographic space, and assessed how well each supports analytical questions about the spread of the virus across Local Authorities in England.
summary.importance: Making the glyphmap design-decision space explicit gives analysts and public communicators a basis for choosing a visualisation whose strengths match their question (timing of peaks, relative magnitudes, synchrony between neighbouring areas), and for understanding the trade-offs (clutter, occlusion, salience bias) that come with each. The provided code makes the same designs reusable for other countries and for phenomena beyond the pandemic where time and place both matter to the analysis.
summary.methods: We developed several glyphmap designs for Covid case data at the Local Authority scale in England, in which a small chart for each area is placed at the area's geographic location. We then formulated a framework of Data Requirements and Design Requirements derived from existing visualisation attempts and from analytical questions about the outbreak, and used the framework to evaluate the designs. The evaluation was supported by an observational data analysis using each design in turn.
summary.findings: Each design exposes different aspects of the spread: some emphasise the timing of peaks across areas, others the relative magnitude of cases, others the synchrony or otherwise of trajectories between neighbouring areas. The framework makes the design-decision space explicit, allowing analysts to choose a glyphmap whose strengths match their question. The paper also identifies the trade-offs inherent in any such design, including clutter, occlusion and salience bias, and provides code so that the designs can be applied to other countries and to phenomena beyond the pandemic.

title: Linguistic and semantic factors in government e-petitions: A comparison between the United Kingdom and the United States of America
authors: Clark, S. D., & Lomax, N.

summary.background: E-petition platforms are now offered by many governments, and a popular petition can shape the political agenda. But the factors that drive popularity have been studied largely on single platforms in single countries, leaving open whether the same linguistic features matter across democratic contexts. This paper replicated an existing US methodology for analysing the linguistic and semantic content of e-petitions on the UK's parliamentary platform, and compared what predicts popularity across the two countries.
summary.importance: Direct replication of a US methodology on the UK platform turns claims about petition popularity into testable cross-country evidence, and shows which mechanisms (structural controls) travel and which (specific linguistic features) are country-specific. That gives platform designers, campaigners and researchers a basis for choosing which insights generalise. The replication framework also adapts to other countries with active petitioning systems, supporting a more cumulative comparative literature on digital democratic participation.
summary.methods: We applied a previously published US-platform methodology to the UK Parliament's e-petitions platform. We modelled the popularity of each petition, measured by signature counts, as a function of structural control variables (such as petition age, time on the platform, and topic categorisation) and of linguistic features extracted from the petition text, including the use of named entities, sentiment and topical content. We then compared the patterns of significance with those reported for the equivalent US platform.
summary.findings: Structural control variables were significant predictors of petition popularity in both countries, suggesting that the basic dynamics of e-petition signing travel across the two contexts. UK petitions were more popular when they included specific named entities in the text. Topical content, by contrast, was more influential in the US. The findings suggest that while the e-petition format generates similar broad dynamics in both countries, the linguistic features that move signature counts differ in ways that reflect national political context. The replication framework can be extended to other countries with petitioning systems.

title: A classification for English primary schools using open data
authors: Clark, S., Lomax, N., & Birkin, M.

summary.background: English primary schools are usually benchmarked against all schools nationally or against schools in the same local authority, even though their pupil composition, neighbourhood and other contextual factors vary widely. Headline comparisons that ignore context penalise schools serving more challenging populations and reward those whose intake makes good results easier to achieve, and no published classification captures the multi-dimensional context in which schools operate. This paper built a classification of English primary schools using open data so that schools can be benchmarked against others that share their context.
summary.importance: Grouping schools by shared multi-dimensional context (pupil composition, staffing, area-level affluence) gives a fairer benchmarking basis than geographic groupings or single-variable adjustments. Parents can read schools against peers facing similar circumstances; school leaders can find genuine comparators for improvement work; local authorities can identify cohorts for targeted collaboration. The interactive map and user guide put the classification in the hands of users beyond the research community.
summary.methods: We used open data on each English mainstream primary school, covering pupil composition (including ethnicity, language and gender), staffing and area-level affluence. We applied a clustering approach to group schools into a small set of distinct types based on shared contextual profiles, then mapped the resulting groups onto neighbourhood characteristics. The classification was published as an interactive map alongside a user guide.
summary.findings: The classification produced a set of recognisable school groups that we describe as "families of schools" with shared contextual profiles. The groups identify clusters of schools that face similar contexts, supporting more nuanced benchmarking and the targeting of collaboration between schools that share starting conditions. The mapping resource makes the classification usable by parents, schools and local authorities. The paper argues that contextual benchmarking is essential if performance assessment is to be both fair and useful.

title: Ravenstein Revisited: The Analysis of Migration, Then and Now
authors: Rees, P., & Lomax, N.

summary.background: Ernst Ravenstein published a set of "laws of migration" in the 1870s and 1880s that still shape how internal migration is taught and researched. But the data Ravenstein used and the questions he could ask were tightly constrained by the censuses of his era, and modern migration research now has access to vastly more detailed data, so the question of which of his observations have stood up and which have been overtaken remains unmapped. This paper compared Ravenstein's approach with how migration is studied today.
summary.importance: A side-by-side reading of Ravenstein's data, methods and findings against today's gives migration researchers a clear sense of which classical observations still anchor the field and which have been overtaken by fixed-interval flows, registers, longitudinal microdata, big data and scenario-based projection. The exercise also serves a teaching purpose: it lets students see why particular concepts (gravity, scale, attribute analysis) came to dominate, and where the open research questions now sit.
summary.methods: This is a comparative review paper. We set out the data and methods Ravenstein used (lifetime migration tables from the 1871 and 1881 censuses of the British Isles, mapped at county level, with concepts of "absorption" and "dispersion") and compared them with contemporary alternatives: fixed-interval census migration questions, registers, surveys, big data, internationally harmonised flow databases, gravity models, methods for handling the modifiable areal unit problem, and microdata permitting analysis of migrant attributes.
summary.findings: Several of Ravenstein's observations anticipate later developments: the dominance of short-distance moves prefigures the gravity model, and his finding that flows run towards "centres of commerce and industry" remains broadly true in most countries, complicated by later phases of suburbanisation, counter-urbanisation and re-urbanisation. Where the field has moved well beyond him is in the study of migrant attributes (age, sex, ethnicity, education, partnership status, social class) using microdata, and in scenario-based projections linking migration to inequality and climate. Ravenstein's framing remains a useful baseline, but the data and methods now available let migration researchers address questions that he could only sketch.

title: The SIPHER Consortium: Introducing the new UK hub for systems science in public health and health economic research
authors: Meier, P., Purshouse, R., Bain, M., Bambra, C., Bentall, R., Birkin, M., Brazier, J., Brennan, A., Bryan, M., Cox, J., Fell, G., Goyder, E., Heppenstall, A., Holmes, J., Hughes, C., Ishaq, A., Kadirkamanathan, V., Lomax, N., Lupton, R., Paisley, S., Smith, K., Stewart, E., Strong, M., Such, E., Tsuchiya, A., & Watkins, C.

summary.background: Improving population health and reducing health inequalities requires coordinated action across the economy, education, welfare, labour markets and housing. But the existing research base is fragmented and not well suited to the cross-sector trade-offs this involves, and no UK research hub had been organised to align evidence across these sectors at the scale strategic decisions need. This open letter introduced the SIPHER Consortium, a UK research initiative that aims to build the evidence base and decision tools that healthy public policy requires.
summary.importance: SIPHER gives the UK an explicit centre of gravity for cross-sector evidence on the wellbeing consequences of upstream policy. Drawing on complex systems science, health economics and policy analysis, the Consortium is sized to produce evidence and decision tools at the scale that strategic decisions require, and its four initial focus areas (inclusive economic growth, adverse childhood experiences, mental wellbeing, housing) are configured so methods are reusable across policy domains. For the field, the contribution is a credible, durable infrastructure for Health in All Policies work.
summary.methods: The Consortium brings together a multi-disciplinary group of researchers from six universities together with three government partners at local, regional and national level, and ten practice partner organisations. The intellectual approach draws on complex systems science, health economics and policy analysis. Methods are designed to be adaptable across policy domains, with four areas selected for initial focus: Inclusive Economic Growth, Adverse Childhood Experiences, Mental Wellbeing and Housing.
summary.findings: The letter sets out four questions the Consortium will work on with policymakers: how upstream policies produce wellbeing, economic and equality outcomes; how to appraise the costs and benefits of investment options across multiple sectors; what the public values and how trade-offs between competing outcomes can be negotiated; and how to create conditions for intelligence-led adaptive policy design. As an introductory piece, it signals a shift in research orientation towards healthy public policy, with the wellbeing impacts of policy choices treated as a central consideration across government sectors.

title: Variations in migration motives over distance
authors: Thomas, M., Gillespie, B., & Lomax, N.

summary.background: Long-distance migration is conventionally understood to be driven by employment or education, while short-distance moves are associated with family or housing adjustments. The empirical evidence for this distinction is thin and rarely tested across countries, so it is unclear whether the conventional account holds universally or is shaped by national context. This paper examined how the motives people give for moving vary with distance in three advanced economies: the UK, Australia and Sweden.
summary.importance: Population projections, service planning and migration modelling rely on assumptions about why people move and how those reasons relate to distance. A three-country test based on nationally representative microdata gives demographers and modellers comparable evidence on which assumptions hold and which need revisiting, particularly around family-driven moves. The harmonised six-category motive classification and the distance smoother are reusable for similar comparisons in other countries with relevant survey data.
summary.methods: We drew on three nationally representative microdata sources: the UK Household Longitudinal Study (2009 to 2018), the Australian Household, Income and Labour Dynamics survey (2001 to 2016), and a Swedish survey of motives conducted in 2007. For each country we classified self-reported reasons for moving into six categories (area, education, employment, family, housing and other) and modelled the prevalence of each motive as a function of the distance moved, using a locally weighted smoother to allow flexibility in the relationship without imposing a parametric form.
summary.findings: The patterns largely confirmed the conventional view: housing was the most commonly cited motive for local moves in all three countries, and employment was prominent for longer-distance moves. Family-related motives, by contrast, did not sort by distance in the expected way. They were important for both short and long-distance moves across all three countries, suggesting that family considerations shape migration decisions across the full distance range. The findings imply that models which treat short and long-distance migration as motivated by entirely different forces will misrepresent why people move, particularly for moves driven by family.

title: Local level estimates of food, drink and tobacco expenditure for Great Britain
authors: James, W. H. M., Lomax, N., & Birkin, M.

summary.background: Patterns of expenditure on food, drink and tobacco vary across small areas in ways that matter for public health, retail planning and environmental impact. But published UK expenditure breakdowns stop at twelve regions, far too coarse for local planning, leaving researchers and policymakers working with regional averages that mask the variation they need to address. This paper produced an open-access archive of local-area expenditure estimates for 106 food, drink and tobacco categories across all Local Authority Districts in Great Britain, covering 2008 to 2016.
summary.importance: A nine-year, LAD-level time series across 106 food, drink and tobacco categories opens up research on access to healthy food, retail siting, alcohol availability and the environmental impact of consumption patterns at the scale local interventions actually run at. Because the dataset is open and the methodology documented, public health, economic, retail and environmental researchers can reuse the same series across studies, supporting cumulative evidence rather than parallel one-off estimates. The framework adapts to other countries with comparable survey and census data.
summary.methods: We used spatial microsimulation to combine area-level socio-demographic data from the census with individual-level expenditure data from the Living Costs and Food Survey. The microsimulation produced synthetic populations whose distribution by relevant socio-demographic characteristics matched the known population of each LAD, and from these synthetic populations we derived expenditure estimates for each of 106 product categories. The procedure was repeated for each year from 2008 to 2016, producing a comparable annual time series at LAD scale.
summary.findings: The archive contains expenditure estimates for 106 food, drink and tobacco categories across 380 LADs for nine consecutive years, with documentation of the underlying methodology and assumptions. The dataset is open access and reusable across public health, economics, retail geography and environmental management research, including questions about access to healthy food, alcohol availability, and the environmental impact of food consumption patterns. The framework generalises to other regions where comparable input data are available.

title: The impacts of international migration on the UK's ethnic populations
authors: Lomax, N., Wohland, P., Rees, P., & Norman, P.
journal: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies

summary.background: The UK was facing significant demographic uncertainty as Brexit negotiations unfolded, with international migration likely to change in volume, composition and source country. Population projections by ethnicity had typically used a single central migration assumption, leaving them poorly suited to a period when migration policy was itself in flux. This paper assessed how plausible international migration scenarios under Brexit might shape the size and ethnic composition of the UK population over the coming decades.
summary.importance: Scenario-based projections give policymakers and service planners across health, education, housing and labour markets a way to read how sensitive the future ethnic composition of the UK is to migration policy choices. Varying both total net international migration and the source-country composition shows where uncertainty concentrates and which groups are most sensitive to migration shifts. The framework supports re-running the same scenarios under different policy assumptions and adapts to similar projection questions for other countries.
summary.methods: We extended a bi-regional cohort-component projection model that tracks each of twelve harmonised ethnic groups through age and sex at Local Authority District scale in England, with Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland modelled at national level. We applied a set of international migration scenarios representing different post-Brexit possibilities, varying both the total volume of net international migration and its composition by source country, and therefore by ethnicity. We compared projected populations and ethnic shares across scenarios to 2061.
summary.findings: The projections show that the future ethnic composition of the UK is sensitive to international migration assumptions, particularly for groups whose populations are sustained by continued inflow. Across all plausible scenarios the UK becomes more ethnically diverse over time, but the speed and geography of that change vary substantially. Lower-migration scenarios slow the growth of overseas-born minority groups noticeably, while leaving the growth of UK-born members of those groups largely intact. The findings argue for scenario-based projection as the norm in periods of policy uncertainty, and for explicit attention to the dependence of UK ethnic composition on international migration policy.

title: Point Pattern Processes and Models
authors: Lomax, N., Malleson, N., & Kieu, L.-M.

summary.background: Spatio-temporal point pattern data, recording where and when discrete events occur, have become widely available across many disciplines, from epidemiology and crime science to seismology and ecology. Point process methods have a long history in statistics, but the literature is fragmented across disciplines and assumes a strong methodological background, so researchers approaching newly available point datasets often lack a single entry point that covers the spatial, temporal and spatio-temporal cases together. This chapter provided an overview of the concepts, models and tools used to analyse point patterns, aimed at readers new to the methods.
summary.importance: A single, accessible reference that maps concepts onto methods and to the kinds of question each can answer lets researchers in epidemiology, crime science, seismology, ecology and other fields apply the same toolkit to whichever events their data record. The chapter makes the assumptions behind homogeneous, non-homogeneous and self-exciting processes explicit, and sets out the trade-offs between visualisation, summary statistics and formal cluster detection. That gives users a basis for choosing methods deliberately rather than by default.
summary.methods: The chapter introduces the basic concepts of spatial point patterns and processes, including complete spatial randomness and the first- and second-order properties used to describe a process. It then sets out the standard generating models (homogeneous and non-homogeneous Poisson processes and self-exciting Hawkes processes) and explains how data from these processes can be simulated. It then covers the methods used to analyse observed point patterns, including approaches to visualisation, similarity quantification, spatial clustering and spatio-temporal cluster detection.
summary.findings: The chapter provides a reference for researchers approaching point pattern analysis, mapping concepts onto methods and onto the kinds of question each method can answer. It distinguishes the assumptions of homogeneous, non-homogeneous and self-exciting processes and shows where each is appropriate, and it sets out the trade-offs between visualisation, summary statistics and formal cluster detection. The treatment is method-agnostic about discipline, with the explicit aim of letting researchers apply the same toolkit to whichever events their data record.

title: Rent/price ratio for English housing sub-markets using matched sales and rental data
authors: Clark, S., & Lomax, N.

summary.background: The ratio between rental income and sales price is one of the most-used signals of housing-market state, closely watched by investors and policymakers. But it is typically reported as an aggregate that masks variation across property types and sub-markets, and without property-level matched data the ratios have been confounded by compositional change in the sales and rental stocks. This paper used a property listings dataset in which the same properties had been listed for both sale and rent to compute rent/price ratios at the individual property level and to model how property and location characteristics shape them.
summary.importance: Property-level matched ratios give investors, policymakers and housing researchers a measure of housing-market state that is not confounded by compositional change in the underlying stocks, and the modelled geography lets users see how the ratio varies within a sub-market across England. Establishing the range of "normal" ratios for particular sub-markets also creates a baseline against which future deviations can be flagged, supporting market monitoring at finer scale than aggregate national figures allow.
summary.methods: We used a property listings dataset for England in which a subset of properties had been listed for both sale and rent within the same period, allowing direct calculation of a rent/price ratio for each. We then estimated a regression model relating the ratio to property characteristics, neighbourhood attributes and location, and used the fitted model to map the geographic distribution of the ratio for one chosen property sub-market across England.
summary.findings: The model consistently supported the hypothesis that more desirable properties and more affluent neighbourhoods have lower rent/price ratios, in line with theory and with anecdote from market participants. The matched data also let us begin to characterise the range of "normal" ratios within particular sub-markets, against which deviations might be flagged. The fitted geography of the ratio for the chosen sub-market shows clear spatial structure consistent with the broader pattern of housing affluence in England. The paper argues that property-level matching is a productive route around the compositional limitations of aggregate ratios, and that the same approach generalises to other property sub-markets.

title: Is adolescent body mass index and waist circumference associated with the food environments surrounding schools and homes? A longitudinal analysis
authors: Green, M. A., Radley, D., Lomax, N., Morris, M. A., & Griffiths, C.

summary.background: Access to unhealthy food around schools and homes has been argued to drive adolescent overweight, and some local authorities now restrict where new fast-food outlets can open. But the empirical evidence is mixed and mostly cross-sectional, so policies are being introduced without strong longitudinal evidence at the individual level. This paper tested whether features of the food environment around schools, homes and the routes between them were associated with measures of adolescent weight status, using longitudinal data on pupils in Leeds.
summary.importance: A longitudinal, individual-level design with repeated weight measurements and consistent exposure definitions across home, school and the routes between them gives the food-environment literature evidence on terms that cross-sectional designs cannot deliver. The findings inform local authorities considering or operating siting restrictions, and the explicit characterisation of exposures at home, school and en route gives an extensible template for similar work in other settings.
summary.methods: We used measurements from secondary schools in Leeds, with each pupil assessed in school year 7 (ages 11 to 12), year 9 (13 to 14) and year 11 (15 to 16). Outcomes were standardised body mass index and standardised waist circumference. The food environment was characterised by the number of fast-food outlets, supermarkets and other retail outlets within a one-kilometre radius of the pupil's home and school, and along the travel route between them within a 500-metre buffer. We fitted multi-level models adjusted for confounders to test the association between food-environment exposures and weight outcomes, and we examined change in weight status between time points.
summary.findings: We found few consistent associations between features of the food environment and adolescent weight status. Where statistically significant associations were detected, the effects were small and in some cases ran in the opposite direction to the policy hypothesis. Analyses of change in weight status between time points produced mostly non-significant or inconsistent results. The findings suggest that policy efforts targeting the food environment around schools, taken alone, are unlikely to make a material difference to the prevalence of adolescent overweight, and that broader strategies are needed alongside.

title: Estimating the outcome of UKs referendum on EU membership using e-petition data and machine learning algorithms
authors: Clark, S. D., Morris, M. A., & Lomax, N.

summary.background: The official results of the 2016 UK referendum on EU membership were reported only at counting-area scale, leaving constituency-level Leave vote shares unknown despite their importance for political analysis. Analysts had to interpolate from counting areas or rely on small-area surveys, with no agreed approach, while e-petition signatures, a near-real-time constituency-scale signal, had not been used as inputs to a calibrated model of vote behaviour. This paper estimated Leave vote share for each Westminster Parliamentary Constituency using e-petition signature data and machine learning.
summary.importance: Constituencies, not counting areas, are the units of UK political representation, so constituency-level Leave shares matter for understanding how MPs interpreted and responded to the referendum result. Calibrating a model of vote behaviour against the boundary-overlapping counting areas turns e-petition signatures into a usable predictor at constituency scale, and the approach generalises to any setting where a political outcome is reported at a coarser geography than the unit of representation. The method's main caveat is also useful: it makes explicit the conditions under which petition activity carries vote signal, so future applications can assess whether those conditions hold.
summary.methods: We used the number of signatures from each Westminster Parliamentary Constituency on e-petitions related to the EU referendum and adjacent issues. We then trained machine learning models to predict Leave vote share from petition signatures together with socio-demographic covariates, calibrating the models against the known Leave shares at counting-area level, where boundary correspondence with constituencies allowed it. The fitted models were used to estimate Leave shares for all constituencies, and the estimates were compared with other published constituency-level estimates derived through different methods.
summary.findings: The petition-and-machine-learning estimates of Leave vote share at constituency level correlated well with other published estimates derived from different sources, suggesting that the petition signal carries useful information about underlying political sentiment at this scale. The approach offers a way to estimate political outcomes at finer geographies than those at which they are officially reported, with the caveat that it depends on petition activity being a reasonable proxy for the underlying preference, which is unlikely to hold equally for all political questions. The method is generalisable to other settings where petitioning is widespread.

title: Ethnic internal migration: The importance of age and migrant status
authors: Darlington-Pollock, F., Lomax, N., & Norman, P.

summary.background: Ethnic minority populations in England and Wales differ in age structure and in time spent in the UK. Most analyses of internal migration treat ethnicity as a single dimension and attribute differences to socioeconomic position, without separating UK-born from overseas-born members of each group, so interpretations of ethnic differences may be misleading. This paper tested whether the determinants of internal migration propensity differ across ethnic groups once age, country of birth and time spent in the UK are taken into account.
summary.importance: Ethnic differences in internal migration propensity feed forecasts of local population change, debates on residential segregation and service planning. Stratifying by age, country of birth and length of UK residence shows which differences survive once those structural factors are taken into account, and which dissolve. That gives researchers and planners a more defensible basis for projecting how ethnic minority populations will move within the UK, and a methodological template for using census microdata to interrogate similar questions about other sub-populations.
summary.methods: We used individual-level microdata from the 2011 Census for England and Wales. We modelled the probability of having made a residential move in the year prior to the census using logistic regression, with covariates including age, ethnic group, country of birth and socioeconomic characteristics. We stratified the analysis by ethnic group, age and country of birth, and we examined separately, for overseas-born members of each group, whether time spent in the UK was associated with the probability of internal migration.
summary.findings: Differences in migration propensity between ethnic groups persisted after stratification by age and country of birth and were not fully explained by socioeconomic differences, contrary to what earlier research had suggested. For overseas-born members of ethnic minority groups, longer time spent in the UK was associated with some of the observed differences in propensity. The findings argue for a more disaggregated treatment of ethnicity in migration analysis, and for service planning that accounts for the joint effect of age, ethnicity and birth status rather than ethnicity alone.

title: A mass-market appraisal of the English housing rental market using a diverse range of modelling techniques
authors: Clark, S. D., & Lomax, N.

summary.background: Automated mass-market appraisal of property is well developed in the sales market, but rare in the rental market even as the private rental sector has grown. The relative performance of different modelling approaches on rental listings had not been compared, leaving landlords, tenants, letting agents and policymakers without guidance on which to use at scale. This paper assessed how well a range of modelling approaches could estimate rental listing prices in England, using over a million listings from a property listings website.
summary.importance: A like-for-like comparison of regression, tree-based machine learning and a practitioner-style approach on the same rental listings dataset gives landlords, tenants, letting agents and policymakers practical guidance on method choice. The finding that the simpler practitioner approach can outperform the more elaborate model on median appraisal error is a useful caution for the wider methodological debate about machine learning versus classical methods in applied valuation work. The framework is reusable for any region with comparable listings data.
summary.methods: We used over 1.2 million private rental property listings collected from a property listings website over two years for England. We modelled rental listing price using three families of approach: generalised linear regression with hedonic predictors, machine learning algorithms (including tree-based methods), and a simpler "pseudo practitioner" approach that mimics how an experienced letting agent might appraise a property. Predictors included the number of rooms, proximity to central London and to railway stations, neighbourhood affluence, local amenities and school performance.
summary.findings: Listing prices were higher for properties with more rooms, closer to central London and to railway stations, in more affluent neighbourhoods, and near better-performing schools and local amenities. Tree-based machine learning algorithms outperformed the regression approaches on standard accuracy metrics. Yet the simpler practitioner-based approach achieved the lowest median appraisal error overall, a useful caution against assuming that more elaborate methods will always do better. The paper offers practical guidance on method choice for rental mass appraisal, and notes that running sophisticated machine learning on data of this scale remains a real computational constraint on standard desktop hardware.

title: Classification of Westminster Parliamentary constituencies using e-petition data
authors: Clark, S., Lomax, N., & Morris, M. A.

summary.background: Politicians need to understand the concerns of their constituents, but conventional polling at constituency level is expensive and slow. Geodemographic classifications of UK constituencies exist, but they have used socioeconomic and demographic characteristics, leaving political sentiment unmapped at this scale. This paper built a classification of Westminster Parliamentary constituencies from the political sentiment expressed through e-petition signatures and assessed how it mapped onto electoral results.
summary.importance: A sentiment-based constituency classification gives politicians, parties and analysts a constituency-level indicator that updates as new petitions accumulate, and complements the standard socioeconomic geodemographics rather than duplicating them. The same workflow runs in any country with a verified-signature petitions platform, so the approach travels to other legislatures with comparable data. The findings also give a concrete demonstration that petition-signing patterns carry coherent political signal, which lifts the analytical value of these data beyond the descriptive use they often receive.
summary.methods: We used the volumes of signatures from each Westminster Parliamentary constituency to the UK Parliament e-petitions that had been debated between July 2015 and February 2017. The petitions covered a range of issues including immigration, education, health, libertarian causes and the EU referendum. We then applied a Gaussian finite mixture model, a probabilistic clustering approach that allocates each constituency to the class whose petition-signing pattern it most resembles, with the number of classes selected by model fit. We mapped the resulting classes against general election results for the same constituencies.
summary.findings: Four distinct classes of constituency emerged from the petition data, labelled Domestic Liberals, International Liberals, Nostalgic Brits and Rural Concerns. The classes corresponded recognisably to electoral patterns: Nostalgic Brits aligned with strongly Leave-voting and more socially conservative areas; the two Liberal classes leant towards Remain and progressive political alignments; Rural Concerns picked up areas dominated by countryside-focused petitions. The findings show that petition data carry meaningful, locally-anchored political signal that complements electoral data, and that the approach can be updated as new petitions accumulate and adapted to other legislatures with similar systems.

title: Temporal Change in Internal Migration in the United Kingdom
authors: Lomax, N., & Stillwell, J.
journal: Internal Migration in the Developed World

summary.background: Long-term internal migration has fallen in the US since the 1970s, prompting questions about whether other developed countries have followed the same path. No single source provides a consistent long-run record of UK internal migration at Local Authority District (LAD) scale, so whether the UK is on a similar trajectory has been hard to answer. This chapter examined how the intensity and patterns of internal migration within the UK changed over time, drawing on census, administrative and survey data together with an estimated inter-LAD annual time series.
