summary.importance: Triangulating across the census, NHS administrative records, the ONS Longitudinal Study and an estimated annual inter-LAD time series gives migration researchers a longitudinal view at LAD scale that no single source supports. That makes it possible to compare the UK's experience with the long-running US decline on like-for-like terms, and to decompose the headline trend by age, by distance and by urban–rural geography. The combined-source approach is itself a contribution: it gives a template for similar long-run analyses elsewhere.
summary.methods: We brought together evidence from three streams: aggregate decadal counts from the UK censuses, longer-run administrative data from the National Health Service Central Register, and microdata from the ONS Longitudinal Study linking individual census records across time. We then drew on our estimated annual inter-Local Authority District (LAD) time series for 2001/02 to 2012/13, which covers all four nations of the UK and supports decomposition by age. We focused on the North–South divide and on flows between urban and rural districts, with particular attention to London.
summary.findings: Internal migration intensity in the UK declined modestly across the period studied, broadly consistent with the longer-running decline observed in the US, although the UK pattern is shaped more strongly by economic cycles. Longer-distance moves fell more than shorter ones. The historic counter-urbanisation pattern persisted but weakened, driven mostly by a fall in moves from urban to rural areas. London remained the hub of the UK migration system, accounting for a large share of both within-system flows and connections with the rest of the country. The chapter underlines the value of building consistent inter-LAD time series by combining the available sources.

title: Circular migration plots
authors: Sander, N., Stillwell, J., & Lomax, N.
journal: The Routledge Handbook of Census Resources, Methods and Applications

summary.background: Visualising migration flows between many origins and many destinations is hard: conventional flow maps overlay lines on geography, and dense flows occlude one another. Migration researchers now have detailed origin–destination matrices, but the standard tools for visualising them have changed little since the nineteenth century, leaving analysts with a choice between simplifying the data or losing the relational structure in numerical summaries. This chapter presented the circular migration plot as an alternative, arranging origins and destinations around a circle and using line width, colour and ordering to encode flow volume, direction and relational distance.
summary.importance: Circular plots reveal the relational structure of a migration system that flow maps obscure, particularly when the matrix is large or flow volumes are very uneven. The technique extends beyond migration to any relational data of similar shape: trade, commodity exchange, citation networks. The chapter also makes explicit the design trade-offs (ordering, thresholds, grouping) that determine whether a plot is useful, giving analysts a checklist rather than a default output to fall back on.
summary.methods: The chapter set out the construction of circular migration plots step by step. Origins and destinations are arranged around the perimeter of a circle in an order chosen to minimise crossings; flow volume is encoded by line width; direction is encoded by colour; and small flows are omitted to keep the plot legible. We discussed the design decisions involved in producing a readable plot, including the choice of zonal ordering, the volume threshold, the role of grouping by region, and the trade-offs between simplicity and information density. The technique was illustrated using UK census migration data.
summary.findings: Circular plots show the structure of a migration system more clearly than conventional flow maps when the matrix is large or when flows of very different volumes coexist, because the relational rather than geographic layout removes line occlusion. The technique generalises to other relational data, including trade, commodity exchange and citation networks. The chapter argues that effective visualisation is a design problem as much as a coding problem, and that producing a useful plot depends on iterative choices about what to include and exclude.

title: Data analytics: on the cusp of using new sources?
authors: Norman, P., Marshall, A., & Lomax, N.

summary.background: Quantitative social science is shifting from the census and large planned surveys towards administrative data and new "Big Data" sources. The strengths and limitations of these sources compare in ways that have not been made plain, leaving researchers without a clear basis for matching source to question. This paper reviewed three styles of data source used to study population and society, and set out where each adds value and where it falls short.
summary.importance: Setting censuses, planned surveys and Big Data side by side gives social scientists and policy analysts a clearer basis for matching source to question, particularly where the substantive stakes are high: health inequalities, educational outcomes, discrimination. The paper argues for Big Data as a complement to traditional sources rather than a replacement, with established data anchoring how the newer sources should be read. That position has direct implications for how research funders and government statisticians invest in data infrastructure over the next decade.
summary.methods: The paper appraised three styles of data source for studying population and society: national censuses, large planned social surveys, and administrative or "Big Data" sources. For each, we discussed what it covers, where it is reliable, and the kinds of question it can and cannot answer. We then considered how the three could be combined to address contemporary research and policy questions.
summary.findings: Big Data has clear potential to clarify how society is changing, particularly because it can capture behaviour at a frequency and granularity that planned surveys cannot. Yet coverage is uneven, definitions are unstable, and interpreting what new sources show requires comparison against established ones. The paper argues that Big Data is most useful when treated as a complement to traditional sources, with the established data providing the anchor against which the newer data are read.

title: Using the 2001 and 2011 Censuses to reconcile ethnic group estimates and components for the intervening decade for English local authority districts
authors: Rees, P., Clark, S., Wohland, P., Lomax, N., & Norman, P.
journal: The Routledge Handbook of Census Resources, Methods and Applications

summary.background: Reliable estimates of population by ethnicity at small-area scale matter for monitoring disadvantage and for grounding projections, but UK demographic statistics have no continuous source of ethnic-group information between censuses. Earlier intercensal estimates rolled forward from one census alone, and when the next census arrived the figures showed substantial drift, particularly for migrant-receiving groups. This chapter reconciled populations and components of change by ethnicity, age and sex for Local Authority Districts (LADs) of England between the 2001 and 2011 censuses, anchored to both endpoints.
summary.importance: Anchoring intercensal estimates to both census endpoints, rather than rolling forward from one, produces component rates by ethnicity that are consistent with all the official data points available. That gives demographers and projection teams informed assumptions to feed into the next round of ethnic population projections, replacing the educated guesses that drove earlier work. The same two-anchor approach generalises to any longitudinal setting where a population characteristic is only observed at intervals.
summary.methods: We treated the 2001 and 2011 censuses as "book ends" and estimated populations and components of change for the intervening years for each LAD in England, with Wales handled as a single zone. The estimates were constrained at each year so that the ethnic breakdown summed to the official mid-year total population and to the official totals for births, deaths, internal migration and international migration. Twelve ethnic groups were harmonised across the two censuses to support consistent comparison. The resulting time series of component rates by ethnicity provides the basis for setting more informed assumptions in subsequent projections.
summary.findings: The chapter sets out a method for producing intercensal time series of population and components of change by ethnicity at LAD scale, with constraints chosen so that the resulting series remain consistent with official aggregates and with both census endpoints. The approach demonstrates the value of building demographic time series around two census anchors, particularly when sub-population information is unavailable between censuses. The methods generalise to other longitudinal settings where a population characteristic is only observed at intervals.

title: Population Projections by Ethnicity: Challenges and Solutions for the United Kingdom
authors: Rees, P., Wohland, P., Norman, P., Lomax, N., & Clark, S.

summary.background: Many developed countries are growing more ethnically diverse, but standard demographic models do not include ethnicity, so how that diversity will evolve at sub-national scale is hard to project. Previous UK projections by ethnicity rested on the 2001 Census base, and no published work had compared 2001- and 2011-based projections to gauge the uncertainty involved. This chapter produced population projections by ethnic group for the UK to 2061, at Local Authority District scale for England and at national level for Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, and assessed how the projections respond to changes in assumptions.
summary.importance: Sub-national projections by ethnicity feed planning across education, housing, health and employment and inform monitoring of disadvantage. By comparing 2001- and 2011-based projections side by side, the chapter quantifies how much of the uncertainty in projected diversity comes from the choice of base year, and where (which areas, which groups) that uncertainty matters most. The bi-regional model and the harmonised 12-group classification are reusable for re-basing at each new census, supporting more transparent projection updates.
summary.methods: We applied a bi-regional cohort-component model that tracks each ethnic group through age and sex over time. Component rates for each group (fertility, mortality, internal migration, international migration) were estimated from census, administrative and survey data. Assumptions were aligned with the most recent official UK projections, with the exception of international migration, where we assumed a higher long-run net balance than the official projection. Twelve ethnic groups, harmonised across the two censuses, were projected through to 2061. We compared projections based on the 2001 and 2011 Census starting points to assess the scale of uncertainty.
summary.findings: The projections show the UK population rising substantially over the period, with the combined Black, Asian and other minority ethnic share rising from under a tenth to around three tenths of the total. Diversity is greatest in the largest cities, but minority populations grow fastest outside those cities, reflecting diffusion. Comparing the two starting points reveals considerable uncertainty in the scale and geography of future diversity, although the direction of travel towards a more diverse UK is clear in both. The work argues for routinely re-basing such projections at each census round.

title: An introduction to microsimulation for demography
authors: Lomax, N., & Smith, A. P.

summary.background: Microsimulation, a family of techniques for estimating characteristics and modelling change for individual units in a population, is widely used in policy analysis but is less familiar to demographers. The existing literature is written largely for a policy-analysis audience, leaving demographers without a clear entry point to a method that is well suited to multi-attribute estimation and projection. This paper introduced microsimulation to demographers through worked examples covering both static population estimation and dynamic projection at small-area scale.
summary.importance: Microsimulation handles multi-attribute population estimation and small-area projection in ways aggregate methods struggle with, but its adoption by demographers has lagged its use in policy analysis. A worked, code-backed demographic example demonstrates the method on familiar demographic objects (age, sex, ethnicity, fertility, mortality, migration) and gives demographers a starting template they can adapt. The accompanying open code and data lower the cost of trying the method on other small-area projection problems in any country with census and survey data.
summary.methods: Using data from the 2011 UK Census, we built a synthetic population for the London Borough of Tower Hamlets cross-classified by age, sex and ethnic group, constraining the synthetic counts to known marginal totals. We then applied dynamic microsimulation to project this synthetic population forward by ten years, allowing individuals to age, give birth, die and migrate according to assumed rates. We visualised the projected population at small-area scale and as a population pyramid. The code and the underlying data are made available so that others can replicate and adapt the procedure.
summary.findings: The worked examples demonstrate that microsimulation handles multi-attribute population estimation and projection at small-area scale in a way that aggregate methods find difficult. The synthetic population for Tower Hamlets matched the constraining marginals and supported decomposition by detailed ethnic group. The dynamic projection generated plausible counts at Middle-layer Super Output Area scale and revealed differences in growth between groups within the borough. The paper argues that microsimulation is an adaptable and underused tool for demographers, well-suited to estimation and projection problems where multiple population attributes need to be tracked, and that the approach generalises to other countries.

title: Changing intensities and spatial patterns of internal migration in the UK
authors: Stillwell, J., Lomax, N., & Chatagnier, S.
journal: The Routledge Handbook of Census Resources, Methods and Applications

summary.background: The UK census is the most reliable source of origin–destination migration data, but changes between rounds in geographies, age bands and definitions have made direct between-census comparison rare. Without that comparison, evidence on whether UK migration intensity has fallen, as it has in the US, rests on administrative time series at much coarser scale, and the question of how sensitive the answer is to scale and zonation has gone untested. This chapter harmonised the 2001 and 2011 Census origin–destination matrices at Local Authority District (LAD) scale, computed migration indicators across the decade by age, and tested their sensitivity to the spatial system used.
summary.importance: Harmonised LAD-scale migration matrices for the two censuses give researchers a like-for-like view of intra-UK migration change across the 2000s, with disaggregation by age included. Pairing the substantive findings with an explicit scale and zonation sensitivity analysis flags how much weight to put on differences between countries or between time periods that use different spatial systems. The chapter both delivers the substantive comparison and arms readers with the diagnostics to interpret similar comparisons elsewhere.
summary.methods: We used 2001 and 2011 Census origin–destination migration matrices at LAD scale for the UK, applied adjustments to harmonise the two rounds, and computed a set of standard migration indicators covering intensity and impact, both for all ages and disaggregated by age group. We then assessed the sensitivity of those indicators to scale and zonation using stepwise aggregation of LADs into larger regions across many alternative configurations.
summary.findings: National migration intensity at LAD scale fell between 2001 and 2011, with the sharpest declines at younger and older ages and milder change in the middle of the working-age range. Patterns of net redistribution also shifted, with continued but weaker counter-urbanisation and a reconfiguration of net flows between the south and the north. The scale and zonation analysis showed that indicators of migration impact were sensitive to the number and shape of the regions used, particularly at coarser scales, with implications for any comparison across countries or across time that uses different spatial systems.

title: Equitable or elitist? The social impact of the 2014 Tour de France Grand Départ
authors: Whittle, M., Lomax, N., Heppenstall, A., & Brerton, S.

summary.background: Mega-events are typically evaluated by economic and visitor headline figures, but who actually attends has rarely been measured. For publicly subsidised events pitched as inclusive, the question matters: if access is uneven, the social legacy claims for these events come under strain. This paper assessed the demographic composition of spectators at the 2014 Tour de France Grand Départ in the UK, testing whether the event drew a representative cross-section of society or skewed towards the stereotypical white, male, middle-aged cycling spectator.
summary.importance: A demographic profile of spectators by route segment turns the legacy debate into something measurable: hosts and policymakers can see which interventions widened access and which sections stayed unrepresentative. The framework is reusable for any large public event with a spectator survey, and the findings give event planners and funders an empirical basis for advance accessibility planning rather than post-hoc justification.
summary.methods: We used a previously unpublished survey of spectators collected during the three days of the 2014 Grand Départ across stages in Yorkshire and between Cambridge and London. We assessed the demographic profile of attendees in terms of age, sex, ethnicity and disability, both overall and by stage of the route, and compared this profile with reference populations to test whether different sections of the event were more or less accessible. We also considered the role of deliberate interventions intended to widen access along certain parts of the route.
summary.findings: The spectator profile skewed white, male and middle-aged, in line with the popular image of the cycling spectator, and the skew was strongest along the least accessible parts of the route. Ethnic minorities and disabled people were under-represented across large parts of the event. Where targeted interventions improved physical access, the demographic profile of spectators came closer to the national population. The findings suggest that the social equitability of large sporting events is shaped by where the event is sited and what is done to widen access, and we argue for systematic advance planning of accessibility in future events of this scale.

title: Estimating Population Attribute Values in a Table: "Get Me Started in" Iterative Proportional Fitting
authors: Lomax, N., & Norman, P.

summary.background: Iterative proportional fitting (IPF) is widely used across population geography and demography to combine incomplete data sets, but the foundational papers are dense and mathematical, and the existing literature applies IPF without teaching it. The result is that researchers new to the technique either avoid it or apply it without understanding how it behaves. This paper provides an accessible introduction to IPF, with worked examples, reproducible code and three case studies drawn from population geography.
summary.importance: IPF underpins many population estimation problems: filling in missing cells in cross-tabulations, scaling small-area data to larger-area constraints, building synthetic populations, and estimating origin–destination matrices for migration. A worked, code-backed introduction lowers the entry barrier for any of those applications, lets researchers diagnose when the method is and is not appropriate (zero cells, mismatched margins, three-plus dimensions), and gives teachers a reusable resource. The three case studies double as starter templates that adapt directly to similar problems in any population geography setting.
summary.methods: We worked through the IPF procedure step by step using a small numerical example, then discussed practical considerations such as convergence criteria, handling of zero cells, integer constraints, and extension to three or more dimensions. We then applied IPF to three case studies drawn from population geography: estimating populations by age and sex for the wards of a local authority district; estimating internal migration flows between areas; and estimating multiple attributes for a local population from a sample distribution constrained by area totals. Code and data for all three are made available so others can reproduce and adapt the procedures.
summary.findings: The case studies show that IPF is practical for a range of geographical data problems, fast in computation, and transparent once the steps are made explicit. The method behaves predictably with appropriate seed values and constraints, but is sensitive to zero cells and to mismatched marginal sums. Across the worked examples, IPF produced reasonable estimates that aligned with the marginal information used to constrain them. The paper argues for treating IPF as an accessible tool that population geographers can use confidently, provided seed and constraint choices are clearly documented.

title: The IMAGE Studio: A Tool for Internal Migration Analysis and Modelling
authors: Stillwell, J., Daras, K., Bell, M., & Lomax, N.

summary.background: Comparing internal migration across countries is hampered by the modifiable areal unit problem: each country reports flows over its own set of sub-national units, and results depend on the scale and shape of those units. Existing software did not let researchers interrogate this dependence systematically, so cross-country comparisons rested on shaky ground. This paper presented the IMAGE Studio, a tool that takes a country's origin–destination matrix, populations at risk and digital boundaries as inputs, and used it to assess how scale and zonation shape comparative findings for the UK, Germany, Sweden and Finland.
summary.importance: The Studio brings together in one environment the full range of migration measures, controlled aggregation of basic spatial units into larger regions, and calibration of spatial interaction models. That makes it possible, for the first time in a single workflow, to separate genuine country-level differences in migration behaviour from artefacts of the spatial system used to measure them. The tool is reusable for any country that can supply an origin–destination matrix, populations at risk and boundary data, and supports both substantive migration research and methodological work on scale and zonation.
summary.methods: The Studio takes a matrix of migration flows between basic spatial units, the populations at risk in each, and the unit boundaries as input. It aggregates the units into larger regions in stepwise scale increments and across many alternative zonal configurations at each scale. For each configuration it computes both system-wide indicators (intensity, connectivity, inequality, mean distance moved) and unit-level indicators, and calibrates a doubly-constrained spatial interaction model, which estimates the frictional effect of distance on flows while respecting known origin and destination totals. We demonstrated the Studio on three UK migration datasets and on comparable data for Germany, Sweden and Finland.
summary.findings: The frictional effect of distance on migration in the UK was relatively stable across scales above around 50 regions, but became unstable below that, while the mean distance moved rose sharply as the number of regions fell. Across the four countries, German migrants were the most distance-sensitive and Swedish migrants moved furthest on average. Finland and Sweden both showed strong scale effects in the distance decay parameter that were absent or muted in the UK and Germany. Zonation effects were larger in the smaller-population countries. The findings demonstrate that what looks like a country-level difference in migration behaviour can be partly an artefact of the spatial system used to measure it, and argue for explicit treatment of scale and zonation in any cross-country comparison.

title: Internal Migration in the United Kingdom: Analysis of an Estimated Inter-District Time Series, 2001–2011
authors: Lomax, N., Stillwell, J., Norman, P., & Rees, P.

summary.background: Internal migration shifts more people around the UK each year than international migration does, yet during the 2000s most attention went to international flows. The dominant account of UK internal migration, centred on counter-urbanisation and the north–south tension, rested on pre-2000 patterns, and no consistent inter-district series existed to test whether those patterns survived the late-2000s recession. This paper used a newly estimated inter-district migration time series for 2001/02 to 2010/11 to trace how internal migration patterns within the UK changed across the decade.
summary.importance: A whole-UK inter-district time series that includes flows across the borders of England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland gives migration researchers, statistics agencies and regional analysts a single, comparable object to interrogate. Set against the standard counter-urbanisation and north–south frames, it shows where those frames still apply and where they need updating in light of the late-2000s recession. The decade-long view also matters for forecasting regional inequality and housing pressure, where the assumptions in use predate the data this paper assembles.
summary.methods: We drew on the inter-district migration time series for 406 Local Authority Districts (LADs) across the UK, estimated from administrative data in each home nation. We computed migration indices covering intensity, distance moved, spatial connectivity, flow inequality and effectiveness across the full decade. We mapped district-level net migration for three twelve-month periods spanning the decade, separating intra-national from cross-border flows. We then summarised flows using two consistent classifications applied across the whole UK: an urban–rural split based on population density, and a north–south divide that includes Scotland and Northern Ireland alongside the more usual England-and-Wales framing.
summary.findings: Migration intensity, distance moved, spatial connectivity and effectiveness all declined across the decade. Counter-urbanisation continued but weakened, driven mostly by a fall in moves from urban to rural districts rather than a rise in the reverse direction. The north–south net balance also shifted: the north was the net gainer in the early years, but by the second half of the decade the south was gaining, largely because of an increase in moves from the urban north to the urban south. Cross-border flows fell in volume and their geographical pattern changed. London remained the principal driver of the UK migration system. Together the findings suggest that the recession of the late 2000s coincided with, and probably contributed to, a slowdown and reconfiguration of the UK internal migration system, with implications for regional inequality and housing pressure in the South East.

title: Subnational migration in the United Kingdom: producing a consistent time series using a combination of available data and estimates
authors: Lomax, N., Norman, P., Rees, P., & Stillwell, J.

summary.background: Migration drives much of the change in local populations across the UK. But the four national statistics agencies produce migration data on different bases, and no single framework brings them together at Local Authority District (LAD) level, so the UK migration system cannot be tracked uniformly across nations or years. This paper constructed a consistent annual time series of LAD-to-LAD migration for the UK from 2001/02 to 2010/11 and used it to trace how migration patterns shifted across the decade.
summary.importance: Treating the UK migration system as a single interaction matrix makes the data architecture explicit: each cell is either populated from agency outputs or estimated, and the procedure for each is documented. That gives statistics agencies and researchers a shared object to reason about when assessing local resource allocation, mid-year population estimates and the cross-border flows that had previously been invisible. The methodology generalises to any country or region where migration data are compiled by separate agencies under different conventions.
summary.methods: We built an interaction matrix of inter-LAD flows covering three components: internal intra-national migration within each home nation, cross-border migration between home nations, and international immigration and emigration for each LAD. Known cells were populated from National Health Service administrative records held by each statistics agency. Unknown cells, principally LAD-to-LAD cross-border flows and Northern Ireland intra-national flows, were estimated using iterative proportional fitting, with the internal cell structure of the 2001 Census as a starting point. We tested the procedure on England and Wales, where official LAD-to-LAD estimates exist, to assess how closely the method reproduced observed flows.
summary.findings: Migration intensity in the UK peaked in the middle of the decade and fell back by 2010/11, broadly tracking the economic cycle. Within-country flows were the most stable over time. Cross-border and international flows showed greater shifts, including a reversal in Scotland from net international loss to net gain by the end of the decade. The long-standing counter-urbanisation pattern of urban losses and rural gains continued but weakened across the period, with notably less redistribution in 2010/11. Net international and net internal migration were negatively correlated across LADs, with London functioning as an international gateway and as a source of internal outflows. The consistent matrix provides a foundation for tracking subnational migration uniformly across the UK in future.
